articles.title: Beyond Consequences of Challenge: the Degree to which Spoken Word Recognition Changes in Response to Difficulty has Independent Relevance
articles.authors: John Baltazar Muegge; Bob McMurray
articles.abstract: Listeners must often recognize words in challenging listening conditions like background noise. The cognitive mechanisms of spoken word recognition offer a potential locus for adaptation to such contexts. Indeed, research has found that the millisecond-by-millisecond dynamics of word recognition in challenging conditions differ lawfully along a small number of dimensions. However, comparatively little is known about the factors that impact the nature of an individual listener’s response to challenge. Here we ask if this response is stable across time and challenge type, if it is constrained by the idiosyncrasies of how listeners recognize words in quiet, and if these patterns of processing predict performance in real-world outcome measures. We tested listeners in a Visual World Paradigm with two different types of challenging listening across two days. We then leveraged a principal component analysis to extract underlying dimensions of variance across these conditions. Using this approach, we found that the dynamics of word recognition in challenge are predicted by their dynamics in typical speech, that these dynamics are stable across days and different types of challenge, and that the magnitude with which listeners change recognition predicts their performance in tests of speech-in-noise comprehension.

articles.title: Predicting Personality Traits from Short Unstructured Conversations with AI
articles.authors: Daniel Robert Lametti; Ileana Wheeler; Jonah Appleton; Robin Murphy; Santiago Castiello
articles.abstract: Given the complexity of personality, we might assume that significant behaviour is required to express our traits. Here we use large language models (LLMs) to test the extent to which personality is visible in short conversations with artificial intelligence (AI). In a preregistered experiment, 100 participants completed the Big-Five Inventory (BFI) before having unstructured conversations with GPT-4.1, writing a median of 430 words. We then instructed a second LLM rater (Claude Sonnet 4.6) to complete the BFI for each participant, predicting their responses based solely on an analysis of the participant-GPT chats. Correlations between LLM-predicted and self-reported BFI traits were significant (range r = .25 to .47), in some cases matching previously documented self-other predictions from family members. A linguistic analysis revealed that the LLM rater’s predictions relied largely on lexical content as opposed to syntax. Using preexisting data, we tested if the AI’s persona influenced how much participants revealed about themselves in conversation. A hundred participants chatted with two versions of GPT-4.1—one that mirrored their personality (mirror AI) and one that opposed it (inverse AI). The LLM rater predicted BFI traits based on the interactions and we correlated this prediction with self-report. Mirror chats generated significant correlations, averaging r = .41; for inverse chats the average fell to r = .30, dropping to zero when the prediction relied on lexical content alone. People readily convey their personality profile in short conversations with AI, and this is enhanced when the AI’s persona mirrors the users.

articles.title: Who with OCD gets referred? A 10-point deprivation gap in English primary care records
articles.authors: Himanshu Tyagi; Mustafa Sarang; Chrissy Jayarajah; Rajeev Kolluri; Nick Sireau; Mark Paramlall
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: 

Psychological treatment and SSRIs are both first-line options for obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) and body dysmorphic disorder (BDD), but whether people in deprived areas receive the same kind of care is unknown. NICE has published tables from English primary care records (CPRD Aurum) for two possibly overlapping cohorts: 20,253 people diagnosed within three years and 7,271 newly diagnosed.

AIMS: 

To establish whether deprivation is associated with which care is recorded, mental health referral or SSRI prescribing, in adults and children.

METHOD: 

We verified NICE's 1,171 values, rebuilt counts from rounded percentages, repeated every test over all admissible counts with multiplicity, clustering and missing-data sensitivity analyses, and compared findings with national prescribing, NHS Talking Therapies data and 25 published studies.

RESULTS: 

Among newly diagnosed adults, 42% in the most deprived fifth had a mental health referral recorded, against 52% in the least, while SSRI prescribing barely differed (61% against 62%). In the three-year cohort, referral was 41% against 48% and SSRI prescribing higher in the most deprived fifth (54% against 49%). The two outcomes' slope indices differed by 17.0 percentage points (three-year cohort; Holm-adjusted P < 0.001) and 15.5 (newly diagnosed; Holm-adjusted P = 0.041; Bonferroni 0.082). NICE's comorbidity-adjusted estimates were similar. In newly diagnosed children, exploratory analyses showed referral of 46% against 54% (odds ratio 0.70 to 0.75), and lower SSRI prescribing in Asian than White children (0.60 to 0.65). In national NHS Talking Therapies data, OCD formed a smaller share of anxiety referrals in areas whose referrals came more from deprived neighbourhoods (Spearman's rho −0.48), unlike generalised anxiety disorder.

CONCLUSIONS: 

In what are, to our knowledge, England's only national primary care data on OCD and BDD, deprived areas had less recorded mental health referral but no less SSRI prescribing: equal prescribing should not be read as equal care. Child differences need confirmation; linked records could show whether the gap is in treatment received.

articles.title: Co-constructed Emotion: A Collective Predictive Coding Theory of Interoception and Social Symbol Sharing
articles.authors: Takato Horii; Chie Hieida; Yuri Terasawa; Ohira Hideki; Tadahiro Taniguchi
articles.abstract: Emotion is both a psychological phenomenon rooted in physiological fluctuations and a socially constructed phenomenon shaped by language and culture. However, traditional psychological constructivism has remained confined to individual brain processes, while social constructivism has lacked a bottom-up computational mechanism explaining how language and culture emerge from bodily emotional substrates and dynamically evolve. To bridge this theoretical gap, this paper proposes the Theory of Co-constructed Emotion (TCoE) via Collective Predictive Coding (CPC), a framework coupling physiological regulation with social symbol sharing within a single active inference formulation. We extend the conventional CPC model by explicitly incorporating interoception---which is indispensable for modeling emotion from a physiological perspective---into each agent's generative model, alongside exteroception and internal and external representations. In TCoE, the co-construction of emotion is described as a dual inference process: an internal loop of allostasis regulating individual bodily states, and a social loop of communication sharing emotional concepts with others. These loops mutually minimize prediction errors mediated by shared symbols (emotion words). We argue that this theoretical framework 1) aligns with psychological findings on emotional contagion and concept formation, 2) enables constructive verification in multi-agent robotic systems, and 3) provides a computational redefinition of psychiatric conditions such as alexithymia as a disconnection between interoception and social symbols. Thus, we offer a novel computational foundation for emotion research that unifies individual embodiment and social symbol systems.

articles.title: Toward a Program Theory of A Singaporean Single-Session, Synchronous Chat-Based Mental Health Support for Youths: The Behavior Change Techniques Workers Use and How They Relate to Outcome
articles.authors: Gerard Chung; Lim Tse Min; Joan R. Fang
articles.abstract:
Background: Text-based chat (TBC) services are among the most accessible mental health
support for youth, yet more is known about whether they help than about how they help, that
is, what workers do in sessions. Without an account of these worker skills, TBC services cannot
be reliably trained for or evaluated. This study described the techniques chat workers use,
drawing on the Behavior Change Technique Taxonomy (BCTTv1), and linked them to user-
reported outcomes.

Methods: We analyzed 1,439 real chat sessions (44,916 worker turns) from 73 workers at
QuickChat, an anonymous, free, synchronous TBC service for youths aged 12 to 25 in Singapore.
Each worker turn was coded for the presence of 32 behavior change techniques (BCTs). We
examined how often, densely, and broadly techniques were used; how far use varied across
workers; and associations with three post-session outcomes: understanding, coping, and
perspective.

Results: All 32 techniques appeared, but practice was concentrated in a few: social support
(unspecified and emotional), problem solving, re-attribution, and framing/reframing accounted
for over half of all instances. Use varied mainly by session, not by worker, indicating skills
shared across the workforce, not individual styles. Three were positively associated with all
outcomes, namely social support (unspecified and emotional) and information about social and
environmental consequences, though effects were small.

Conclusions: Chat workers deliver change through a small set of core skills, centered on social
support and shared across the workforce. These findings offer a first step toward a program
theory of TBC to guide training and evaluation.

articles.title: Bridging Languages, Rebuilding Communication: Best Practices for Assessing and Treating Discourse for Bilingual People with Aphasia
articles.authors: Danielle Fahey; M K Niharika; Reem S. W. Alyahya; Saryu Sharma
articles.abstract: A considerable proportion of the global adult population is bilingual; however, research on aphasia and language processing remains predominantly centered on monolingual speakers, leading to reduced understanding and guidance about bilingual aphasia. Bilingual aphasia is not equivalent to monolingual aphasia, as bilinguals process each language differently from monolinguals. As such, they are likely to have different error patterns and recovery processes. Best practice for assessing bilingual individuals with aphasia requires evaluating all languages they have sufficiently acquired. Because standardized normative tools are not available for many language combinations or even for numerous individual languages, clinicians can derive necessary insights into a bilingual patient’s linguistic strengths and impairments through systematic discourse sampling. Consequently, we provide best practice recommendations for assessing and treating discourse production in bilingual aphasia. We synthesize current practices in language assessment and treatment of discourse production for bilingual aphasia populations, and provide clinically applicable recommendations for selecting, administering, coding, and interpreting discourse assessments across languages. We also provide recommendations for selecting and adapting discourse interventions, treatment languages, and cross-language targets within the constraints of multilingual clinical service delivery.

articles.title: The Nature of Phonological Impairments in Dyslexia and Stuttering: Evidence from Phonemic, Semantic, and Design Fluency Tasks
articles.authors: Mahmoud Medhat Elsherif; James H Smith-Spark; Richard Kirkden
articles.abstract:
Objectives: Using executive fluency tasks, the current study investigated whether these challenges reflect phonological representations themselves or access to intact representations during self-reported adults who stutter (AWS) and self-reported dyslexic adults.
Method: An online, unsupervised sample of 62 self-reported AWS, 62 self-reported dyslexic adults and 62 neurotypical adults completed a modified, typed version of semantic and phonemic fluency, as well as a mouse-drawn version of design fluency. We analyzed switching (shifting between subcategories; proxy for retrieval efficiency) and cluster size (words per subcategory, proxy for representational integrity). 
Results: Controlling for nonverbal IQ and language measures, hierarchical regression showed that dyslexia and stuttering significantly predicted reduced overall phonemic output, whereas semantic and design fluency remained unaffected. Both groups showed reduced switching, though more pronounced in the dyslexia group. Conversely, only stuttering predicted reduced cluster size.
Conclusion: Given the heterogeneity of these neurodivergent profiles, these findings suggest that, in dyslexia, access to phonological representations is affected. Conversely, stuttering affects the representations themselves. For individuals presenting these specific cognitive signatures, interventions could be tailored toward either retrieval strategies or representational strengthening.

articles.title: What Makes a Match? Evaluating Visual and Textual Information in Dating Apps' Profiles
articles.authors: Anna Gerna; Marco Marini; Fabio Paglieri; MarcoViola
articles.abstract: Online dating platforms require users to evaluate potential partners based on sparse, highly curated information, typically profile pictures and short self-descriptions. The present study examined how characteristics of visual and textual cues in dating profiles shape overall desirability (i.e., dateability), focusing on physical attractiveness (for photos) or interest (for bios), alongside likability, trustworthiness, and self-confidence. Participants evaluated photos and bios from simulated Tinder profiles, rating these dimensions together with their willingness to date the target. Linear mixed-effects models revealed that, although physical attractiveness and perceived interest were the strongest predictors of willingness to date the target for photos and bios, respectively, other dimensions also played an important role. Crucially, observed associations varied with participants’ gender and prior dating app experience. Gender differences in photo-based evaluations were largely concentrated among experienced users, suggesting that evaluative strategies may differ more with familiarity with dating platforms’ dynamics than by gender alone. Experience was also related to differences in the evaluation of bios, with inexperienced users placing more importance on perceived trustworthiness and self-confidence. Beyond these substantive findings, the study provides an openly available set of ecologically grounded dating-profile stimuli, both visual and textual, empirically characterized across multiple dimensions relevant to social and romantic evaluation. These materials may provide a useful resource for future research on online dating and the integration of visual and textual social information in digital profiles.

articles.title: Personalizing Structured Self-Help in the Moment: Students’ Experiences With Embedded AI Chatbots in a Guided Digital Mental Health Platform
articles.authors: Sascha Y Struijs
articles.abstract:
Background: University students can use guided digital mental health interventions without having immediate access to a coach. Fixed programme content does not always answer questions about choosing a programme or applying an exercise to a personal situation. This study examined whether purpose-specific large language model chatbots can address this gap within an existing platform, MoodLift. The study focused on how students judged their usefulness, trustworthiness, and safety.
Methods: Two prototypes developed for MoodLift were evaluated: a Program Selection Assistant and an AI Coach. Ten first-year students used both tools. They completed usability and acceptability measures before joining one of two focus groups. Questionnaire results were summarized descriptively. Focus-group transcripts were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis.
Results: Mean Chatbot Usability Questionnaire scores were 70.3 for the Program Selection Assistant and 70.8 for the AI Coach. Acceptability ratings were generally positive. Five themes were developed: (1) from general self-help to personal support; (2) providing direction while preserving autonomy; (3) students trusted the chatbots conditionally, not automatically; (4) embedding made AI more relevant and legitimate; and (5) safety required a bounded, complementary role. Situational fit emerged as a cross-cutting principle: preferences varied between students and depended on the task and context.
Conclusions: Purpose-specific chatbots can help students use guided digital self-help at the moment questions arise. Their value depends on reliable responses and an explicit scope. Providers should explain how data are handled and who remains responsible, while ensuring that human support is available

articles.title: From Behavioral Instructions to Perceptual Goals: Manipulating Anthropomorphism in Human-AI Communication Experiments
articles.authors: Xingman Wu
articles.abstract: Researchers commonly manipulate chatbot anthropomorphism through social cues, whose effects vary and may introduce unintended perceptual differences. Generative AI enables an alternative: manipulating perceived characteristics through natural-language prompting. Two online experiments (N = 84 each) evaluated behavior-prescriptive and perception-goal prompting for manipulating anthropomorphism. Study 1 found no significant differences in anthropomorphism. Study 2 found significant differences in general, mindful, and mindless anthropomorphism (ds = .86–.95), without significant differences in response coherence or perceived intelligence. These findings provide initial empirical support for perception-goal prompting and suggest broader methodological possibilities for manipulating perceived chatbot characteristics in human–AI communication research.

articles.title: Toward a More Inclusive Motivation Science
articles.authors: Franki Y. H. Kung; Ziqi Yao; Zhixu (Rick) Yang; Aryca Woodson; Dante Raymond Raymond Bruno; Abigail Scholer; Amanda Diekman
articles.abstract: Good science has the power to move and change lives. At its best, motivation science not only deepens the understanding of human behavior but also contributes meaningfully to improving the lives of people and communities. Central to its excellence is the field’s capacity to speak to a broad spectrum of contexts and human experiences. In this chapter, we reflected on the current state of motivation science by discussing its historical emphasis on universality and considering how greater attention to specificity can further advance the field. We then outlined three promising directions for future development and offer recommendations to support sustainable and systemic change. By moving toward a more inclusive motivation science, we hope to enhance both the field’s knowledge and its community, strengthening a discipline that more accurately reflects and effectively serves the diverse populations it aims to understand.

articles.title: Does Daily Meditation Increase Self-Compassion? A Bayesian Multilevel Diary Study
articles.authors: Matthew J Monnot
articles.abstract:
Evaluations of brief self-compassion programs usually compare phases, leaving open whether 
meditation and nonmeditation days differ. With few nonmeditation days, subtracting each 
person's observed average can distort the separation of day-level from person-level effects. This 
secondary analysis used the archival 28-day diary of 65 employees in a two-week online self
compassion meditation program, with morning reports of meditation over the previous 24 hours 
(Li et al., 2021). Across 14 intervention days, a prespecified Bayesian two-level model treated 
each person's meditation propensity as latent, separating the within-person contrast between 
meditation and nonmeditation days from stable differences in meditation frequency. Hypotheses 
were higher same-day self-compassion on meditation days (primary) and lower next-day 
emotional exhaustion, adjusting for same-day exhaustion (secondary). Results are posterior 
medians, 95% credible intervals (CrIs), and directional probabilities. For same-day self
compassion, the meditation-day slope had median = 0.00 SD, 95% CrI [−0.09, 0.09], P(b > 0) = 
.48; for next-day exhaustion, the slope had median = −0.03 SD, 95% CrI [−0.16, 0.11], P(b < 0) 
= .65. Both CrIs spanned zero. An archival intervention diary can answer an adherence question 
its original phase-based analysis did not ask.

articles.title: Expertise Shapes the Multidimensional Perception of Stories
articles.authors: Qingzhi Ruby Zeng; Derek Lilienthal; Coraline Rinn Iordan; Aaron Steven White; Elise A. Piazza
articles.abstract: Storytelling is a primary means of human connection and creative expression, but it is unclear how mechanisms of story perception may vary across people with differing expertise. Here, we examined how expertise in creative storytelling shapes ratings of five dimensions of story quality (creativity, imagination, novelty, complexity, cohesiveness), as well as how these ratings are influenced by four linguistic feature categories (language productivity, lexical predictability, semantic similarity, and lexical composition). Online storytellers (N=18) improvised six spoken stories each (for a total of 108 stories). The transcript of each story was rated by both novices (N=10-31) and creative writing/storytelling experts (N=15) on the five story dimensions and analyzed using the four linguistic feature categories above. Overall, experts and novices provided similar average ratings, and their rating spaces both showed two distinct underlying principal components–essentially, creativity and cohesiveness–which were, in turn, predicted by distinct linguistic features. However, experts perceived the five dimensions as more differentiated, and their ratings were less driven by linguistic features than novices’. These findings indicate that experts’ judgments are more nuanced but also may rely less on fine-grained structural features of narratives, highlighting the importance of capturing individual differences and multidimensionality in story perception.

articles.title: Modifiable Psychological Variables as Predictors of Return to Work: Temporal Patterns in a Longitudinal Observational Study
articles.authors: Magnus Johansson; Alice Giöstad; Aleksandra Bujacz; Anna Ek; Petter Gustavsson; Lars-Göran Öst; Anna Finnes
articles.abstract:
Background: Common mental disorders (CMDs), including depression, anxiety, and adjustment disorders, are leading causes of long-term sickness absence (SA) and work disability in high-income countries. Despite the significant burden, evidence-based interventions to support return to work (RTW) remain limited. This study aimed to investigate the predictive role of selected modifiable psychological factors on RTW among individuals on sick leave for CMDs, with particular emphasis on temporal dynamics during the early phase of the RTW process. 

Methods: A longitudinal observational study was conducted with bi-weekly self-reported questionnaire measurements for 3 months and quarterly follow-ups for 12 months. Outcomes were self-reported RTW and registry-based net SA days (NSAD). Analyses included robust linear mixed models for focal predictor trajectories, Bayesian logistic regression with a regularizing horseshoe prior for the probability of RTW, and ordered beta regression for NSAD since sick-days data have lower and upper bounds. 

Results: Baseline measurements of RTW-SE and Work Ability Scores (WAS) were also associated with RTW at three months. Improvement in RTW self-efficacy (RTW-SE) during the first three months showed the strongest and most consistent association with increased probability of RTW, both cross-sectionally at 3, 6, and 12 months, and longitudinally.  

Improvement regarding physical fatigue and WAS were associated with approximately 18% less NSAD at 3 and 6 months, while cognitive exhaustion showed similar impact but only at three months.

articles.title: Post-Encoding Semantic Processing Produces Systematic Distortions in Episodic Memory
articles.authors: Katelyn G. Cliver; Kennedy N King; Alexa Tompary
articles.abstract: How new experiences can update a memory has important consequences for its long-term storage, but little is known about how different kinds of re exposure may differentially influence its content. Inspired by theories of memory reconstruction that posit that memory retrieval depends on the integration of idiosyncratic details and relevant general knowledge, we investigated how exposure to a memory through category- or item-level processing may strengthen its episodic and semantic components. Across three behavioral experiments, participants encoded image-location associations in a protocol designed to generate a conflict between memory for specific images and knowledge of the general location of other images from the same category. Following learning of the locations, participants completed manipulations aimed to prioritize category-level or item-level processing of the images. We hypothesized that requiring semantic processing after learning would reinforce prior category knowledge associated with each image and increase category-driven distortions in memory at test. Our findings revealed that memory for images that underwent semantic processing were less precise and more distorted relative to memories that underwent item-level processing and relative to those that were not re-exposed after encoding. Furthermore, post-encoding manipulations more strongly updated memories of atypical category members, suggesting that the organization of prior knowledge can govern the extent that new memories can be updated. Together, these results highlight the active role of post‑encoding manipulations in differentially reshaping memory content and provide compelling evidence that episodic memory retrieval is a constructive process that integrates across prior knowledge, discrete experiences, and subsequent re-exposure.

articles.title: Specifying Innateness in Infant Development: A Framework for Theory-Building Based on Co-Determination
articles.authors: Leher Singh
articles.abstract: Infant research has often treated early neural and behavioral expression as a privileged window into the initial state of the mind, with early-emerging capacities sometimes uncritically taken as evidence of innate knowledge. This paper evaluates the strength of such inferences through four intersecting lenses: genetics and epigenetics, cultural evolution, definitional precision, and standards of scientific explanation and falsifiability. It distinguishes among several non-equivalent forms of innateness, including claims about representational content, architectural or processing biases, developmental canalization, and maturational timing. In place of broad or underspecified appeals to innateness, it advances co-determination as a framework for theory-building that encourages specification of the biological constraints, experiential inputs, cultural ecologies, developmental timing, and interactive mechanisms proposed to produce a given outcome, as well as the patterns of variation that would support or challenge those claims. The central aim is to provide a more precise and testable basis for theorizing about the initial state of the infant mind.

articles.title: Mouthing in comprehension of multimodal multilingual units in Norwegian Sign Language
articles.authors: Felicia Bisnath; Maren Sørhaug; Benjamin Anible
articles.abstract: Mouthings -- mouth movements that mimic spoken language words produced alongside signing -- are a unique multimodal phenomenon in that they recruit resources from a second language; however, they have not received much attention in research that explicitly frames itself as multimodal. In Norwegian Sign Language (NSL/NTS), the role of mouthing in comprehension has not been studied extensively from the perspective of deaf users of the language. In this study, we add to these two understudied areas by exploring mouthings in comprehension of Norwegian Sign Language in an unrestricted lexical identification paradigm (N=30). We find that when manual forms are polysemous, plausible mouthings improve accuracy in lexical identification and the certainty of comprehension. When mouthings are implausible, it appears that the dominant strategy is to make identification decisions based on the manual form only. In a smaller number of cases participants appeared to rely solely on the mouthing or blended the mouthing and manual components.

articles.title: Identifying Discrepancies Between Measurements of Visual, Felt Presence and Tactile, Judged Presence
articles.authors: Oliver Singleton; Marianna Obrist; Aikaterini Fotopoulou
articles.abstract:
Unlike other screen-based technologies such as computer monitors, virtual reality (VR)
systems allow the user to feel a sense of presence – the sense that they are actually
situated within the surrounding virtual environment. Although the foundational experience of
existing within a physical environment goes far beyond aspects of vision, our study is the
first, to our knowledge, to operationalise and measure different facets of the
multidimensional concept of the SOOP, ranging from indirect, trial-by-trial measures of
reaction times and accuracy to higher-order aspects of presence judgements such as their
trial-by-trial metacognitive efficiency, and to modality-specific and modality-general global
(i.e. across many trials), retrospective self-report measures. We primarily hypothesised that
whilst multisensory stimulation is the most important factor in the creation of presence,
unisensory touch will be a greater causative factor in the creation of presence than
unisensory vision. 44 participants completed an implicit reaction-time task (reacting to target
stimuli) and an explicit metacognitive task (rating confidence in object presence). We
manipulated sense type (unisensory vs multisensory), sensory modality (vision vs touch) and
temporal order (e.g., touch-first vs. vision-first). Results indicated that multisensory
integration significantly enhanced metacognitive efficacy, accuracy and reaction speeds
compared to unisensory conditions. However, a key dissociation emerged between
unisensory modalities. While participants reacted faster to visual stimuli, they achieved
higher perceptual accuracy with tactile stimuli, with participants retrospectively rating touch
as feeling significantly more "real" than vision. These findings support the notion that realtime "felt" presence and retrospective "judged" presence may be caused by distinct factors.

articles.title: Power-law Behaviour in Eye Movements During Reading in 21 Languages
articles.authors: Thomas Fabian
articles.abstract: Eye movements provide insights into psychological processes. In reading research, investigating cognitive processes via differences in reading behaviour is prevalent. However, cross-linguistic universalities in eye movement behaviour during reading remain largely unknown. A recent study analysed relations between successive eye movements, designated relative saccade lengths, and found that the relations' probability distributions observe a power-law-shaped tail across various tasks and experiments, including reading in six different languages. Validating this finding and assessing its universality for further languages is essential since it could represent the first language-independent and quantifiable statistical regularity in reading behaviour. With existing data from the MECO corpus, we replicate the original study's results with further empirical data for the same six languages and extend the analyses to a total of 21 languages (N = 1299). The results show that the probability distributions of relative saccade lengths consistently observe a power-law-shaped tail across all 21 languages. Thus, our results replicate the findings of the original study's six languages and extend them to 15 further languages. This provides further empirical evidence for the probability distribution of relative saccade lengths as a possible universality in eye movement behaviour during reading. Furthermore, the slope of the probability distributions suggests that adjusting eye movement lengths during reading might constitute optimal search behaviour.

articles.title: Cognitive Abilities and Trust Calibration: Understanding Individual Differences in Automation Trust Dynamics
articles.authors: Connie Ku; Anne Collins McLaughlin; Richard Pak; Randall W Engle
articles.abstract:
Individual differences in cognitive abilities may influence how people develop and maintain trust
in automated systems, yet the mechanisms underlying this relationship remain poorly
understood. This study investigated how three foundational cognitive abilities — working
memory (WM), attention control (AC), and fluid intelligence (Gf) — shape trust dynamics,
particularly focusing on trust decline and recovery after automation failures. Participants (n=111)
completed cognitive tests measuring WM, AC, and Gf before performing a dual-task paradigm
where they monitored an automated memory aid exhibiting varying reliability levels (100%-
65%-100%) while completing a mental arithmetic task. Results revealed that WM and Gf
positively predicted trust recovery after automation failures, while AC influenced long-term trust
calibration, with high-AC individuals showing more nuanced trust adjustments reflecting system
reliability history. Trust decline was uniform across ability levels, suggesting immediacy of trust
loss. The relationship between abilities and trust may have been partially mediated by
automation schemas, with WM negatively correlating with all-or-none thinking about
automation. These findings suggest different cognitive abilities play distinct roles in trust
dynamics: WM supports monitoring automation performance, Gf enables effective schema
updating, and AC facilitates appropriate deployment of these resources for trust calibration. This
work advances our understanding of trust mechanisms and has implications for designing
automation interfaces that accommodate individual cognitive differences.

articles.title: Further Psychometric Evaluation of the Propensity to Trust in Automation (PTT-A) Scale and Validation of a German Version.
articles.authors: David Scholz; Johannes Kraus
articles.abstract: The Propensity to Trust in Automation (PTT-A) scale by Scholz et al. (2025) provides a psychometrically sound instrument for assessing individual differences in the propensity to trust in automated systems. To date, however, the scale has only been validated in its original English version. The present study aimed to validate both the 14-item and 6-item versions of the scale in German. Furthermore, given the lack of validated measures of PTT-A with established measurement invariance (MI) across languages and gender, we examined whether the scale permits meaningful comparisons across these groups, thereby facilitating cross-cultural research on trust in automation. To this end, the PTT-A scale was translated into German, and its psychometric properties were evaluated in a large-scale online study (N = 1,629). In addition to examining the German versions, we assessed the psychometric properties of the original English versions and tested MI across language (English vs. German) and gender (female vs. male) using multigroup confirmatory factor analysis. The results supported the psychometric properties of both the 14-item and 6-item versions in English and German. Furthermore, sufficient MI was established across language and gender, supporting the comparability of scale scores between the respective groups. Overall, the findings provide a validated German version of the PTT-A scale in both its full and short forms. The evidence for MI across language and gender further supports its use in cross-language research and comparisons of propensity to trust in automation across these groups.

articles.title: Human likeness is a misplaced benchmark for artificial intelligence
articles.authors: Valerio Capraro; Gary Marcus; Walter Quattrociocchi
articles.abstract: Recent claims that large language models pass the Turing test span different procedures, but share a common focus on human outputs, rather than the processes that lead to those outputs. Here we challenge the inference from successful imitation to intelligence. Similar outputs can arise from different processes and conceal differences in reasoning, generalization, and adaptation. More fundamentally, we question whether human likeness should guide AI development at all. Prioritizing imitation can reproduce human biases, facilitate manipulation, and favor replacing people over augmenting their capabilities. AI systems should expand human welfare, not merely impersonate us. We recommend three coordinated changes: designing systems that strengthen human capabilities and independent judgment; requiring funded projects to assess benefits, costs, and their distribution; and guiding institutional procurement and renewal by evidence of AI’s effects on human welfare.

articles.title: A climate policy referendum decreases pluralistic ignorance on climate change concern
articles.authors: Viktoria Cologna; Jana Freundt; Eugenia Bajet Mestre; Niels G. Mede; Lauren Christine Howe; Jamie Lee Gloor; Eri Bertsou; Naomi Oreskes; Reto Knutti; Mike S. Schäfer
articles.abstract: Pluralistic ignorance about others’ climate change concern can contribute to inaction on climate change. We conducted a two-wave panel study (Npre = 1,578, Npost = 827) with a general sample before and after the national Swiss referendum on the Climate Protection Law, which was accepted. We find that people underestimate others’ concern about climate change and others’ support of scientists’ policy advocacy. Pluralistic ignorance of climate change concern slightly decreased after the referendum, while pluralistic ignorance of scientists’ advocacy remained unchanged. Results thus show that national voting on climate policy creates a window of opportunity that can be harnessed to reduce pluralistic ignorance.

articles.title: The Formation of the Sufferer: Deconstructive Inquiry and the Self-Problem Relation in Psychotherapy
articles.authors: Arie Todd Greenleaf
articles.abstract: Psychotherapy generally begins with a person who has a problem and needs help resolving it. Deconstructive Inquiry (DI) examines how the struggle to resolve a difficulty can form the apparent self who must overcome it. This conceptual paper draws on a relational ontology, which understands things as organized patterns of relations. The self who must overcome fear, for example, takes shape through judging, resisting, and trying to escape fear. This activity is experienced as someone separate from the feeling and responsible for ending it. I call this formation centering. Comparison with a remembered past or imagined future can sustain the struggle by making present life unacceptable until the person changes. DI proposes that the effort and its apparent controller can become recognizable as the same activity. The division need not continue, even while fear remains and the person responds to what needs attention. A composite clinical vignette illustrates this possibility and shows how the therapist’s need to prove helpful can reinforce the client’s struggle. I also propose that insight changes the knowledge shaping later encounters, allowing change to persist without requiring the person to recall or repeat the insight. Comparisons with other therapies examine whether a separate observing self remains when therapy succeeds. The paper considers how cultural expectations shape these struggles and how therapists and supervisors can participate in sustaining or questioning them.

articles.title: Elected by the face? Facial impressions of honesty and competence made under suboptimal conditions predict voting intentions
articles.authors: Antonio Olivera-LaRosa; Guido Corradi; Sergio Barbosa; Sissy Delgado-Pacheco; William Jimenez-Leal; Gonzalo Luna-Cortes; Javier Villacampa; Jaume Rosselló
articles.abstract: Rapid judgments based on political candidates' facial features often predict electoral outcomes. Building on this, we explored how facial impressions of honesty and competence—formed under suboptimal processing conditions—predict voting intentions for actual political candidates. In this study, 484 participants (Colombians: 199; Peruvians: 285; male: 30.2%) were exposed to candidate faces from Colombia and Peru under time constraints (33 ms or 100 ms). Participants rated these faces on honesty and competence and subsequently indicated their likelihood of voting for each candidate. Our findings demonstrate that while rapid facial impressions predict voting preferences overall, this effect is strongly amplified when candidates are recognized from one's own country, whereas for foreign candidates, the relationship remains minimal or disappears. Crucially, because voting intentions were evaluated during subsequent unconstrained viewing, these rapid impressions interact with full-viewing processing rather than acting in complete isolation. By utilizing real candidate photographs, this study confirms that rapid facial impressions align with electoral preferences in naturalistic settings, operating through an integrated process where familiar faces instantly retrieve pre-existing political attitudes.

articles.title: The Emotion Filmmaker: Temporal Memory, Time-Emotion Integration, and Affective Style
articles.authors: Mengsi Li; Regina C Lapate
articles.abstract: Emotional experiences are temporally dynamic, but prior work suggests that temporal features are usually neglected in remembered emotion. For instance, retrospective emotion evaluations are often biased by discrete salient timepoints, such as the peak and end moments, at the expense of objective event duration (i.e., peak–end effects and duration neglect). However, how these retrospective emotion biases originate, as well as their significance for emotional functioning, remain unclear. Here, we test the hypothesis that retrospective emotion biases are related to fundamental limits of temporal processing and memory capacity. Further, we examine whether these limits have implications for emotional functioning. Participants (n = 60) underwent a novel paradigm comprising affectively-rich movie sequences while providing emotion ratings continuously (moment-by-moment) and retrospectively. Temporal memory for previously-watched emotional-movie sequences and dispositional negativity were measured. Our findings revealed a greater “end” bias as the duration of emotional-movie sequences increased, suggesting that limitations in temporal processing capacity may contribute to retrospective emotion biases. Critically, temporal-memory errors were associated with larger retrospective emotion biases and with individual differences in dispositional negativity. Collectively, these results indicate that retrospective emotion biases may stem partly from mnemonic temporal errors that are emotionally maladaptive.

articles.title: Commitment-Driven Information Seeking in Misinformation Consumption
articles.authors: Alessandro Miani; Théo Schöpfer; Stephan Lewandowsky; Thomas Hills; Adrian Bangerter
articles.abstract: The role of social media in misinformation consumption remains contested. This disagreement might arise from the failure to distinguish incidental exposure to misinformation from deliberate consumption. We address this gap by analyzing incoming traffic data, collected in November 2020, to more than 2,000 websites that vary in misinformation and type of bias (liberal, conservative, and conspiracy). We compare the traffic modalities through which users reach those sites: direct traffic, such as typing a URL or using a bookmark (mostly associated with self-directed information seeking); social traffic, from links clicked on social media; and search traffic, from search engines (mostly associated with incidental exposure). We found that reliable, low-misinformation websites are reached mainly via search traffic, whereas unreliable ones are mostly reached via direct traffic; this pattern is stronger for conspiracy websites. Breaking down social traffic by platform reveals that Facebook was the main driver of traffic towards unreliable websites, mostly towards politically biased and entry-level conspiracy websites. These findings suggest that structural interventions such as algorithmic adjustments and content moderation may reduce incidental exposure among users with low belief commitment, but are unlikely to deter highly committed information seekers, who require targeted, ideologically informed strategies.

articles.title: Is a joke funnier if it is told by a man? A novel paradigm using AI-generated voices
articles.authors: Amy Zhao
articles.abstract: The stereotype that “men are funnier than women” is culturally pervasive. In a large preregistered online study (n=966), participants rated 12 jokes delivered by a male or female AI-generated voice. To control for differences in delivery, cadence, and intonation, we used a speech-to-speech transformation to transform jokes spoken by a female into a male version and vice versa. Using a Bayesian analysis, we found strong evidence that the apparent gender of the speaker does not affect the perceived funniness of the joke (BF=0.023). We found no interaction between the original and apparent voice gender on masculinity ratings, indicating that vocal gender cues were effectively eliminated when voices were transformed to the opposite gender, reinforcing the merit of this gender manipulation method. Further, men had significantly higher agreement that being funny is a masculine trait than women (MD=0.73, padj<.001), and participants with more male than female friends had significantly higher agreement with this belief than those with equal numbers of male and female friends (MD=0.68, padj<.001) or more female than male friends (MD=0.91, padj<.001). In all, apparent vocal gender does not appear to influence humour evaluations directly, but exploratory findings suggest the apparent vocal gender and delivery may shape broader impressions of speakers (such as perceived confidence and charisma). And individual differences such as gender and proportion of male friends may shape gendered attitudes and expectations toward humour.

articles_hidden.title: Empirical Signatures of Choice-Induced Preference Change
articles_hidden.authors: Douglas G. Lee; Giovanni Pezzulo
articles_hidden.abstract: Choice-induced preference change refers to the tendency for value estimates to differ after a choice relative to before it. Although this phenomenon is robust, the process that generates it remains debated. In this work, we reanalyzed pooled data from two previous studies to identify empirical signatures to serve as benchmarks for candidate process accounts of choice-induced preference change. We focused on three factors that are especially informative for theory: choice difficulty, deliberation time, and the attribute structure of the options. First, we reproduced the well-established finding that the spreading of alternatives is greater for more difficult choices. Second, we showed that its relationship with response time remains after controlling for difficulty, indicating that the relationship with deliberation time is not reducible to initial value difference alone. Third, we found that preference change depends not only on overall value difference but also on how the options differ in terms of their attributes, with stronger effects for choices laden with tradeoffs than for cases of simple dominance. Together, these results indicate that choice-induced preference change is tied to deliberation itself rather than to a post hoc or artifactual revision of fixed values. The findings are compatible with both value-refinement and coherence-based reasoning accounts in some respects, but they also constrain both by showing that preference change depends jointly on difficulty, deliberation time, and attribute structure.

articles_hidden.title: Breaking the Stasis in the Polyvagal Controversy: Two Category Errors, a Missing Variable, and a Measured Boundary
articles_hidden.authors: Gabriel Kram; Heather MacDuffie
articles_hidden.abstract: For twenty years, the dispute over Polyvagal Theory (PVT) has turned on whether the profound bradycardia attributed to dorsal vagal shutdown occurs in ordinary human freezing and dissociation. The 2026 Grossman–Porges exchange sharpened that dispute without resolving it. We argue that it cannot be resolved as framed, because neither position specifies the variable that would adjudicate it: the pervading neurochemistry under which a recruited circuit operates. PVT made the required observation once, in 2001, when it paired oxytocin-conditioned calm immobilization with vasopressin-conditioned immobilized fear at identical dorsal vagal anatomy. The observation was never generalized, because the neurochemical model PVT inherits retains a two-pole structure in which the endogenous opioids have no position. We propose a three-variable model in which neuroception selects the circuitry recruited and modulatory chemistry determines what that circuitry produces. As a falsifiable hypothesis, severable from the model, we propose that the cardiac and respiratory signature of life-threat immobilization requires endogenous µ-opioid activity, and that naloxone administered during confirmed shutdown should reverse bradycardia and restore respiration on the timescale of the drug’s onset. Independently of the model, electron-microscopic fiber counts of human vagal tissue show that the supradiaphragmatic/subdiaphragmatic discontinuity is confined to the myelinated population, placing that partition on direct measurement rather than comparative inference. Because escapability rather than phylogenetic age selects the state, PVT’s clinical claims do not depend on its evolutionary reconstruction. The observations of both parties describe physiologically distinct conditions, and the model, drawn from Autonomics, converts a twenty-year standoff into experimentally decidable predictions.

articles_hidden.title: Does Outcome Utility Bias the Mental Simulations of Risky Events?
articles_hidden.authors: Yun-Xiao Li; Johanna Falben; Lucas Castillo; Jake Spicer; Jian-Qiao Zhu; Stella Qian; Nick Chater; Adam N Sanborn
articles_hidden.abstract: Does the utility of an outcome influence people's assessment of risk and uncertainty? Prominent theories propose that people rely on mental simulation to evaluate probabilities and risky events, yet prior empirical findings is mixed as to whether and how utility biases this process. Across four experiments (total N=206, with Experiment 4 pre-registered), we tested this question using a random generation paradigm, in which participants mentally simulated gamble outcomes and said them out loud. Then we compared these responses with probability judgments and predictions. While we identified individual differences, the majority of participants exhibited neutrality, with no systematic impact of utility on their sampling distributions. Nevertheless, an optimism subgroup emerged, with a larger proportion of optimistic participants when the monetary context was more salient. Additionally, outcome utilities have similar effects on probability judgments, predictions, and random generation tasks, consistent with the proposal that these tasks are related to each other and may all rely on mental simulation. These findings indicate that utility does not uniformly distort mental simulation, but can do so for a stable subgroup under particular motivational contexts, and they motivate cognitive models that capture both unbiased and optimistic forms of mental sampling.

articles_hidden.title: The Emergent Structure of Memory Phenomenology Depends on Whether Memories Are More Episodic or Semantic
articles_hidden.authors: Tabatha Blaney-Gale; Jordan Poppenk
articles_hidden.abstract: Phenomenological characteristics are central to theoretical distinctions among modern memory constructs. The scene construction framework proposes that episodic remembering involves the construction of coherent scenes, such that the structure of phenomenology may reflect the engagement of the hippocampus and related regions during recall. However, most phenomenology research relies on instruments with content and scoring schemes that embed theoretical assumptions into their measurements. Here, we explored whether phenomenological characteristics emerge from self-reported memory experiences as anticipated by episodic memory theory. We solicited memories from a large online sample, following each response with a novel questionnaire designed to evaluate the phenomenology of individual memories. We used folded bottom-up factor analyses to examine and validate the global latent factor structure of participants’ memory experiences. Consistent with Tulving’s declarative memory framework, our analyses produced five stable dimensions: imagery, autonoetic consciousness, mental time travel, relational memory, and semantic memory. In order, these dimensions reflect multi-modal perceptual reexperiencing, personal meaning, sense of reliving, detailed spatiotemporal context, and conscious use of semantic knowledge during recall. The semantic memory dimension has no clear predecessor, suggesting the strategic use of general knowledge during recall is a distinct and previously uncharacterized aspect of remembering. This factor structure generalized across memories elicited by recent and remote episodic prompts. However, distinct versions of mental time travel and relational memory emerged in response to the semantic prompt, suggesting these dimensions of memory are context-sensitive rather than fixed. While our findings validate the link between episodic memory and its theorized phenomenological elements, they also invite broader investigation of how phenomenology may vary across different classes of memory.

articles_hidden.title: When Creativity Goes Rogue:  Semantic Organization in Conspiracy Thinkers and Politically Extreme Individuals
articles_hidden.authors: Dina Mohamed; Steven Verheyen
articles_hidden.abstract: This study addresses a gap in previous research by examining how semantic memory organization relates to conspiracy endorsement and political extremism. A total of N = 98 participants completed the Generic Conspiracist Beliefs (GCB) scale and an animal verbal fluency task (M_age= 27.88, 〖SD〗_age = 11.45; 59.18% female; 69.39% European). Of these, n = 96 also completed a self-placement political extremism item. Participants were grouped according to their levels of conspiracy thinking (high or low) and political extremity (moderate or extreme). We hypothesized that 1) political extremism would predict conspiracy thinking, 2) that individuals high in conspiracy thinking would exhibit flexible semantic networks, similar to those found in creative individuals, and that 3) politically extreme participants would exhibit similar semantic patterns to participants high in conspiracy thinking. Semantic networks were constructed from verbal fluency responses, and we compared the respective group networks’ clustering coefficient (CC), average shortest path length (ASPL), modularity (Q), and small-world-ness (S). Results showed that political extremism negatively predicted conspiracy thinking. High conspiracists exhibited more flexible semantic networks, consistent with patterns previously observed in creative individuals. Politically extreme individuals showed efficient global connectivity but lacked local associative clustering. These findings suggest that semantic memory structure is meaningfully linked to conspiratorial and ideological beliefs. Longitudinal research is needed to clarify the causal direction of these associations.

articles_hidden.title: On the size of the model selection problem in a conjoint measurement experiment
articles_hidden.authors: Kenneth Knoblauch; Frederic Devinck
articles_hidden.abstract: We examine how the number of models respecting marginality in model selection using Maximum Likelihood Conjoint Measurement (MLCM) varies with the number of dimensions tested and explain the logic for determining this number.  The results are related to Dedekind numbers, which increase super-exponentially, and, thus, suggest a limit to the number of dimensions that can be practically tested using the MLCM paradigm.

articles_hidden.title: Voluntary Challenge, Hallucination, Imagery, and Motor Mindful Scale (VCHIMMS)
articles_hidden.authors: Kevin Sheldrake; Zoltan Dienes
articles_hidden.abstract: The Voluntary Challenge, Hallucination, Imagery, and Motor Mindful Scale (VCHIMMS) is a reformulation of the Challenge, Hallucination, Imagery, and Motor Suggestion Scale (Sheldrake & Dienes, 2026) as instructions for mindful, voluntary behaviour, as opposed to imaginative suggestions for automatic, involuntary behaviour.

articles_hidden.title: Challenge, Hallucination, Imagery, and Motor Suggestion Scale (CHIMSS)
articles_hidden.authors: Kevin Sheldrake; Zoltan Dienes
articles_hidden.abstract:
The Challenge, Hallucination, Imagery, and Motor Suggestion Scale (CHIMSS) is a novel set of imaginative suggestions that each demand the utilisation of phenomenological control. This scale consists of three suggestions of each type: motor suggestions for arm levitation, hands coming together, and head nodding; challenge suggestions for hands stuck together, fingers stuck together, and arm immobilisation; imagery involvement suggestions for a beach scene, an animal-identification scene, and a future scene; and hallucination suggestions for a mosquito, two tastes, and hearing a song playing automatically. The scale notably excludes suggestions for amnesia, post-hypnotic behaviour, and visual hallucinations. It also includes three alternative imagery involvement suggestions that can be used in place of the existing ones or in addition: a meadow scene, a woods scene, and a scene involving identification with a celestial being or superhero.
The introduction script and suggestions were modified from the Phenomenological Control Scale (Lush et al., 2021). The imagery involvement suggestions were modelled after the Imagery Involvement/Dissociation suggestion in the Elkins Hypnotizability Scale (Elkins, 2013, pp. 99–124).

articles_hidden.title: When Does Reputation Help the Future? Audience Presence and Identity Disclosure in Intergenerational Resource Dilemmas
articles_hidden.authors: Mingyuan Sheng; Ye Niu; Xiaoli Ling
articles_hidden.abstract: Many environmental problems, from climate change to resource depletion, are intergenerational dilemmas: the present generation bears conservation costs, whereas the benefits go to future generations, who can neither observe nor reciprocate. Reputation reliably sustains cooperation among contemporaries, but whether it works across generations remains unclear. In two experiments using an intergenerational goods game, we examined how the audience of disclosure and the type of information disclosed affect contributions to a resource passed from one generation to the next, and whether social value orientation (SVO) moderates these effects. In Experiment 1, disclosing to the next generation what participants had contributed increased the rate of sustained generations but did not reliably increase individual contributions or narrow the gap between prosocial and proself individuals. In Experiment 2, disclosing the same information to present peers increased both individual contributions and the rate of sustained generations. Adding names and faces was tentatively associated with a further increase in contributions, although this condition was recruited in a separate wave. These gains came mainly from proself individuals, whose contributions no longer differed from those of prosocial individuals when names and faces were disclosed. The findings suggest that disclosure promotes intergenerational cooperation chiefly when it reaches an audience present at the time of decision, and that identifiability matters most for those least motivated to cooperate. Making conservation visible to future generations may not be enough; it may also need to be visible to someone now, suggesting a potentially low-cost approach to promoting environmental cooperation.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond the Battlefield: A Cross-Sectional Study of War-Related Stressors and Mental Health in Four Central European Countries
articles_hidden.authors: Piotr Długosz
articles_hidden.abstract:
Prolonged armed conflicts may affect mental health beyond the battlefield through indirect, war-related stressors. However, evidence on populations outside the immediate conflict zone remains limited. This study assessed psychological distress, anxiety, and depressive symptoms and examined their associations with coping strategies among adults in four Central European countries more than two and a half years after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
A cross-sectional online survey was conducted in October 2024 with 2,962 participants from Poland (n = 728), Czechia (n = 743), Slovakia (n = 742), and Hungary (n = 749). Participants were recruited from opt-in online research panels using stratified quota sampling based on sociodemographic characteristics. Psychological distress, anxiety, and depressive symptoms were measured using the Kessler Psychological Distress Scale (K10), the Generalized Anxiety Disorder scale (GAD-7), and the Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-9), respectively. Between-country differences were examined using one-way analysis of variance, and associated factors were assessed using country-specific linear regression models.
Poland had the highest mean scores for psychological distress, anxiety, and depressive symptoms (K10: F(3, 2,958) = 12.61; GAD-7: F(3, 2,958) = 9.40; PHQ-9: F(3, 2,958) = 7.10; all p < 0.001). Czechia had the lowest mean scores for distress and anxiety. Mean depressive symptom scores were lower in Czechia, Slovakia, and Hungary than in Poland, with no significant differences among the three countries. The average item-level selection rate was higher for problem-focused than for emotion-focused strategies in all four countries. Younger age, lower perceived quality of life, and greater use of emotion-focused coping were associated with higher symptom scores. Problem-focused coping was associated with lower symptom scores only in Poland.
Mental health symptom scores differed across the four countries, as did some associations between coping strategies and mental health. The findings support continued monitoring and attention to groups reporting poorer outcomes. Given the cross-sectional design, the observed associations do not establish causal effects.
Keywords: Transboundary mental health; armed conflict; psychological distress; anxiety; depression; coping strategies; Russia–Ukraine war; Central Europe.

articles_hidden.title: From Behavioral Design to Behavior-Based Design: Functional Specification for Designed Environments
articles_hidden.authors: Francesco Di Nocera
articles_hidden.abstract: Behavioral design has developed frameworks and taxonomies that help researchers and practitioners organize, select, and describe interventions. However, identifying an intervention technique does not establish the functional relations through which it influences behavior. This article proposes behavior-based design (BBD) as a programmatic approach that places functional specification at the center of the design process. BBD does not introduce new behavioral principles or replace established methods of behavior analysis. Instead, it organizes their application to deliberately designed environments, including digital interfaces, public services, sustainability initiatives, and organizational systems. The article identifies five criteria for adequate functional specification: behavioral precision, functional coherence, discriminability among alternative functional explanations, relevance to design decisions, and empirical accountability. Examples illustrate how the same intervention category may involve different functional relations, leading to different predictions, measurement strategies, and design decisions. Particular attention is given to competing contingencies, maintenance, generalization, and the conditions affecting those responsible for implementing and sustaining interventions. Finally, the article outlines a research agenda for comparing designs informed by explicit functional hypotheses with approaches relying primarily on broader intervention categories. The proposed contribution of BBD is therefore methodological and programmatic: to make functional specification an explicit requirement of design and to evaluate its predictive and practical value through cumulative empirical research.

articles_hidden.title: Depression-Anxiety Comorbidity Across Sex During COVID-19: An Evaluation of Partial Invariance with Invariance Partial Pruning
articles_hidden.authors: Xinkai Du; Asle Hoffart; Sacha Epskamp; Helga Ask; Ragnar Nesvåg; Sverre Urnes Johnson
articles_hidden.abstract: Depression and anxiety co-occur so frequently that comorbidity is more prevalent than the occurrence of either in isolation. The conventional latent-variable perspective offers limited insight into comorbidity because its inherent causal assumptions overlook causal relations among observable symptoms that are meaningful for explaining comorbidity. At the same time, comorbidity studies based on the network perspective have largely relied on cross-sectional data, which cannot capture the dynamic nature of mental disorders, or on two-wave panel data, which does not separate between- and within-variance and biases the estimation of dynamic processes. Therefore, we present a dynamic network analysis of depression-anxiety comorbidity with the panel graphical vector autoregressive model, using invariance partial pruning to consider possible network structural differences between biological sex. Results revealed the central role of fear in predicting depressive moods and anhedonia as a possible explanation of comorbidity. Anxiety symptoms temporally preceded depression symptoms. In the contemporaneous networks, nervousness and fear were connected to depressive mood. Furthermore, worry and rumination were more associated with depression, whereas beliefs about the uncontrollability of worry and threat monitoring were more associated with anxiety. No sex difference was discovered.

articles_hidden.title: Cognitive Control as a Brake on the Depression–Internet Addiction Link: Task-Based fMRI Evidence from Activation and Task-Modulated Functional Connectivity
articles_hidden.authors: JIAJIA ZHU; Tianxiang Jiang; Lawrence Hoc Nang Fong; Anise Wu
articles_hidden.abstract: Internet addiction is closely associated with negative emotions such as depression, and cognitive control has been proposed to moderate this relationship. However, the underlying neural mechanisms remain unclear. Using a publicly available fMRI dataset, this study examined whether cognitive control-related brain activation and task-modulated functional connectivity (TMFC) moderate the association between depressive symptoms and Internet addiction. Thirty-four participants completed a global–local attention allocation task during fMRI, the Internet Addiction Test (IAT), and Beck Depression Inventory (BDI). Behaviorally, accuracy under conflict conditions negatively moderated the BDI–IAT association. At the neural level, activation in the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and left ventromedial prefrontal cortex negatively moderated this association, whereas activation in the right substantia nigra, right nucleus accumbens, and right caudate nucleus positively moderated it. At the network level, stronger functional connectivity between the frontoparietal control network and the subcortical network weakened the positive BDI–IAT association. These findings suggest that prefrontal regions and frontoparietal–subcortical connectivity may buffer the depression–Internet addiction link, whereas subcortical reward- and habit-related regions may amplify it, providing neuroimaging support for the I-PACE model.

articles_hidden.title: On Great Ape Personality Structure: Problems in Minkov (2026)
articles_hidden.authors: Alexander Weiss
articles_hidden.abstract: A recent paper (Minkov, 2026) claimed that great ape personality is not well-described by the five personality dimensions found in humans, those being Neuroticism, Extraversion, Openness to Experience, Agreeableness, and Conscientiousness. To support this claim, the author analyzed personality factor structures obtained in studies of great apes in which personality was assessed using rating scales. The analyses tested for ‘configural invariance’ by computing the percentage of traits that loaded on the same factor as in humans in chimpanzees, orangutans, mountain gorillas, and bonobos, and the percentage of traits that loaded on the same factor across four studies of chimpanzees. The paper also reviewed the evidence for Conscientiousness in chimpanzees, including by citing the results of studies that used other ratings scales, and concluded that this factor’s evidentiary basis was weak. The paper concluded by proposing an alternative approach to studying personality in great apes. This commentary exposes fundamental problems with the article. First, I show that the paper’s author mischaracterized the research program of comparative psychologists who study personality. Second, I review the evidence the paper uses to support its claim that there is little evidence for configural invariance, highlighting problems and errors in the analyses and reporting of results. Third, I review the evidence presented against the presence of Conscientiousness in chimpanzees and find it problematic. Finally, I demonstrate that the literature review lacks due care. I conclude by dispelling a misunderstanding about comparative research on personality and reaffirm the importance and promise of pluralism in the study of the phenomenon.

articles_hidden.title: NICE’s 2026 Consultation Draft Guideline for OCD and BDD (GID-NG10435): A Critical Appraisal with Secondary Analysis of NICE’s Published Data
articles_hidden.authors: Himanshu Tyagi; Mark Paramlall
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background. In September 2026 the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) opened consultation on the first batch of its update to the 2005 guideline for obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) and body dysmorphic disorder (BDD) (GID-NG10435). The draft replaces stepped care with matched care and reviews first-line treatment.

Methods. We appraised the draft and its supporting documents against six questions informed by selected AGREE II domains, analysing NICE’s published effect estimates, sample sizes, sensitivity analyses and economic results descriptively; every value was checked against its source document. Comparison guidelines were identified by a documented search.

Results. The adult OCD review included 82 randomised controlled trials and the BDD review 13 studies. The committee cited small samples and wide credible intervals when it did not recommend metacognitive therapy (52 participants) or eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing (EMDR; 59 participants). Self-administered cognitive behavioural therapy with therapist support, the second adult option, rests on 61 participants, with a wider credible interval than EMDR’s, and was recommended on other documented grounds. The top-ranked adult option had a probability of 0.17 of being the most cost-effective. The first-listed BDD option ranked fifth of nine in the network meta-analysis. The draft gives no drug-specific dose targets, no consolidated definition of an adequate trial and no primary severity measure for allocation or response. Treatment after non-response to an adequate trial is outside the scope of Batch 1; on the assumptions in NHS England’s 2013 specification, a cascade beginning with 48 million adults in England and Wales yields approximately 48,000 people not responding to a serotonin reuptake inhibitor followed by local graduated exposure. All six selected multimodal OCD comparison guidelines address augmentation; none provides a treatment pathway for BDD.

Conclusions. The draft rests on a substantial evidence synthesis. The published rationale does not fully explain why small samples and imprecision precluded recommendations for some treatments but not others; several operational parameters are not specified; and further-line treatment is outside the first batch.

articles_hidden.title: Neuroscience-Informed Psychoeducation for Bipolar Disorder
articles_hidden.authors: Abigail Ortiz
articles_hidden.abstract: Neuroscience-informed psychoeducation (NIPE) extends traditional psychoeducation for bipolar disorder by grounding clinical content in the neural mechanisms underlying the illness. This chapter reviews the neuroscience foundation relevant to bipolar disorder, including prefrontal-limbic circuit dysfunction, reward processing abnormalities that shift between mood states, circadian rhythm disruption, autonomic dysregulation, and the neuroplastic changes linked to illness progression and recovery. We translate these mechanisms into accessible psychoeducational content addressing diagnosis, pathogenesis, risk factors, and treatment, and describe brain-based strategies spanning cognitive monitoring, circadian-focused interventions, and emerging digital phenotyping tools. Delivery considerations are addressed with attention to the state-dependent nature of insight and cognitive function across mood episodes, phenotype-specific personalization, and family involvement. We outline mechanisms through which NIPE may improve outcomes, including enhanced awareness, reduced stigma, improved treatment adherence, and greater self-efficacy. While empirical evaluation of NIPE specifically for bipolar disorder remains limited, the chapter identifies priorities for future research, including randomized trials, mechanistic mediation analyses, and precision medicine approaches tailored to bipolar phenotype and illness course.

articles_hidden.title: Toward Sensory Accounts of Autistic Masking: A Perspective
articles_hidden.authors: Rebecca Poulsen; Melanie Heyworth; Timothy Chan; Diana Weiting Tan
articles_hidden.abstract: Autistic masking has typically been understood as the suppression of natural Autistic traits within neuronormative social contexts. However, social interactions are inherently embedded within broader sensory environments, highlighting the need to consider how sensory experiences shape masking processes. Although sensory experiences have been recognized within existing masking research, the sensory dimensions of masking remain comparatively underexplored. In this perspective, we examine sensory masking as an interrelated dimension of broader Autistic masking processes, defined as the conscious or subconscious suppression, inhibition, or override of sensory responses to meet environmental or social expectations. Drawing on recent research and our own lived experience, we describe how these sensory dimensions may emerge developmentally, often as a learned adaptation to unsafe or invalidating experiences. We then consider the cumulative effects of sustained sensory masking. While sensory masking may serve a functional purpose, its chronic and persistent engagement may contribute to burnout and negatively impact well-being and mental health, particularly in the context of prolonged exposure to sensory aversive environments. We also distinguish these sensory dimensions from related processes of sensory self-regulation and sensory unmasking, which involve supporting regulation and reclaiming autonomy through safe sensory self-expression. We conclude by outlining constructive approaches that support sensory safety, self-regulation, and well-being, and propose future research directions to explore the mechanisms, impacts, and potential supports associated with the sensory dimensions of masking.

articles_hidden.title: Postpartum Depression Risk Following Exposure to Universal and Unconditional Perinatal Cash Transfers
articles_hidden.authors: Crystal L. Cederna; Rachel Hollander; Jenny LaChance; Sumit Agarwal; Mason Hambley; Eric Finegood; Maya Wolock; Rachel Ablir; Shannon Coughlin; Sooin Choi
articles_hidden.abstract:
Purpose. Postpartum depression (PPD) disproportionately affects women experiencing socioeconomic hardship. We examined the association between exposure to Rx Kids, the nation’s first universal and unconditional perinatal cash transfer program, and PPD risk among mothers of one-month-old infants. 

Methods. This study used Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) data collected from electronic health records of 815 one-month well-child visits between 2022 and 2025, spanning two years before and after Rx Kids implementation. Difference-in-differences analyses compared changes in depression screening outcomes among mothers residing in Flint, Michigan, where Rx Kids was implemented, with changes among mothers residing outside Flint. 

Results. In the two years before Rx Kids, the prevalence of high risk PPD scores > 13 was 8.7% in Flint and 6.2% outside Flint; two years after, the prevalence was 3.3% in Flint and 10.4% outside Flint. Rx Kids exposure was associated with a 9.8-percentage-point reduction in high risk PPD scores (95% CI, -16.8 to -2.8, p = 0.006), reversing the preexisting geographic disparity. Reductions were also observed in moderate PPD risk and mean EPDS scores.

Conclusions. Findings suggest that universal and unconditional perinatal cash support may be an effective upstream strategy for preventing PPD, improving maternal mental health, and reducing place-based disparities.

articles_hidden.title: Can callous-unemotional (CU) traits be acquired? Tests in a longitudinal sample spanning late childhood through adolescence in the ABCD study
articles_hidden.authors: Emily C. Kemp; Meghan Dontha; Zeying Du; Herry Patel; William E. Pelham
articles_hidden.abstract: Background. Callous-unemotional (CU) traits (i.e., “Limited Prosocial Emotions”) characterize a particularly severe group of antisocial youth. “Secondary” CU traits, as opposed to “primary,” are distinguished by co-occurring anxiety and are theorized to reflect an acquired phenotype that develops through an interaction between heightened emotional sensitivity and prolonged adversity exposure. The aim of this study was to test this pathway in a large, diverse sample spanning late childhood (age 9-10) to middle adolescence. Methods. Data were drawn from the Adolescent Brain and Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study, with youth (N = 11, 880; Mage = 10; 48% female) assessed annually over five timepoints. Retrospective and prospective analyses examined the effects of emotional sensitivity and different forms of adversity on the development of CU traits. Results. Retrospective analyses showed no main or interactive effects of emotional sensitivity and adversity during late childhood in predicting secondary CU traits by adolescence.
