Instead, a significant interaction (B = .21, SE = .06, p < .001, RRR = 1.24) was found such that higher overall adversity and emotional sensitivity together increased risk for primary, not secondary, CU traits. Prospective analyses among emotionally sensitive (≥90th percentile) youth with no CU traits (n = 365, age ~10) similarly showed no forms of cumulative adversity predicted increases in or the onset of “elevated” CU traits after four years. Conclusions. Findings did not support a distinct adversity-linked pathway to secondary CU traits via emotional sensitivity. Instead, results were consistent with alternative models in which secondary CU traits reflect a comorbid profile marked by broader clinical severity or overlapping liabilities (e.g., negative affectivity, internalizing risk).

articles_hidden.title: Developing and Validating a Measurement Scale to Assess Knowledge of Memory and Learning Processes Among Italian Teachers
articles_hidden.authors: Francesco Carabba; Ottavia M. Epifania; Demis Basso
articles_hidden.abstract:
Knowledge of memory and learning processes may inform teachers’ educational decisions. However, to our knowledge, no psychometrically validated instrument specifically assesses teachers’ procedural knowledge of these processes through realistic classroom scenarios.
This Stage 1 Registered Report aims to develop and validate a scenario-based measure of Italian teachers’ procedural knowledge of memory and learning processes.
Approximately 600 Italian teachers, from preschool to upper-secondary education, will be recruited through proportional stratified quota sampling based on sex, geographical area, and school level.
Following two pilot studies and iterative revisions, 30 original items were retained and paired with conceptually matched items to create two intended parallel forms. All participants will complete the 60 multiple-choice items online. Exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses will be conducted separately for each form in independent subsamples. Measurement invariance across forms will be examined if corresponding factor structures are supported. Internal consistency will be estimated using Cronbach’s alpha. Mixed-effects logistic regression will examine associations between item-level accuracy and teaching experience, educational attainment, and, among teachers with tertiary qualifications, academic field.
We expect interpretable, replicable factor structures and adequate internal consistency, with measurement invariance providing additional evidence of comparability across forms. Higher accuracy is tentatively expected with higher educational attainment, psycho-pedagogical qualifications, and fewer years of teaching experience.
The study will provide initial evidence on the psychometric properties of the proposed measure. If the findings support its validity and reliability, the instrument could subsequently be used to identify teachers’ knowledge gaps and inform teacher education initiatives.

articles_hidden.title: Effectiveness of Stepped Care Psychological Interventions in Children and Adolescents: A Meta-Analytic Review
articles_hidden.authors: Bianca A. Simonsmeier; Maren Rogawski; Elena von Wirth
articles_hidden.abstract: Stepped care has been proposed as an efficient and scalable framework for delivering pediatric psychotherapy. This meta-analysis examined the effectiveness, generalizability, and implementation characteristics of stepped care interventions for the prevention and treatment of mental health problems in children and adolescents. Across included studies, stepped care interventions demonstrated large significant overall pre–post improvements in health outcomes (d = 1.22, 95% CI [0.944; 1.50]). When compared with control conditions effects were small and non-significant (d = 0.09, 95% CI [-0.133; 0.313]) suggesting that stepped care yields outcomes comparable to standard care including intensive treatments rather than superior clinical effects. Moderator analyses indicated that stepped care effects were largely consistent across patient characteristics, outcomes and methodological qualities. Importantly, stepped care interventions were associated with significantly lower costs compared to control conditions, highlighting their economic advantage. Most studies combined relatively intensive steps, with limited use of self-directed, low-intensity, scalable interventions as initial treatment components. Stepping decisions were primarily based on disorder-specific symptom measures, although some studies incorporated shared decision-making involving clinicians, patients, and families. Exploratory analyses revealed that approximately 46% of the patients transitioned from the initial step, independent of age, and timing of the decision point. Overall, outcomes of stepped care in pediatric psychotherapy appear clinically comparable to usual care while offering substantial cost benefits. The findings support its promise as an efficient service delivery model while underscoring the need for further research on potential barriers and optimal implementation strategies in clinical practice.

articles_hidden.title: Multimodal processing of chemical representations: advantages of chemistry expertise and inadvertent challenges for learning
articles_hidden.authors: Amanda Bongers; Steven Ganescu
articles_hidden.abstract: Chemists use verbal and visual representations of molecules to communicate and solve problems, yet little is known about how chemists efficiently interpret them simultaneously with ease. Participants (N = 200) of varied chemistry expertise completed an experiment in which they solved short representation-matching tasks with bond-line structures and IUPAC names of organic molecules. Drawing upon information-processing theory and prior chemistry education research on representational processing efficiency, we examined how expertise and varied task characteristics affected visual scanning efficiency. We recorded participants’ eye movements during the tasks to quantify the extent to which their gaze was focused or exploratory using a metric called stationary gaze entropy. Chemistry experts exhibited more focused gaze within the bond-line structures presented, which suggests that they more efficiently apply more chunk stimuli and activate prior knowledge connecting the representations. By looking at the effects of varied structural features and complexity, we outline inadvertent challenges that chemistry novices may face while processing these representations during chemistry instruction. We offer chemistry instructors suggestions for mitigating demands on their students’ working memory. We also propose avenues for follow-up research that will allow chemistry instructors to better understand how to scaffold their students’ development of the implicit skills associated with chemistry expertise.

articles_hidden.title: An Elaborated Model of Youth Externalizing Psychopathology
articles_hidden.authors: Irwin Waldman; Holly E Poore
articles_hidden.abstract: Externalizing is an integral spectrum in hierarchical dimensional models of psychopathology. Comprehensive models of Externalizing have been developed for late adolescents and adults, but not for youth. We developed and characterized an elaborated model of youth Externalizing psychopathology using item response theory and confirmatory factor analyses of ADHD, ODD, and CD symptoms to investigate the psychometric properties of Externalizing’s components. Participants included large population-representative twin and clinic-referred samples of youth. Using several criteria, increasingly elaborated models comprising an Externalizing dimension and seven fine-grained symptom factors outperformed models containing omnibus ADHD, ODD, and CD symptom dimensions. Results replicated across clinic and twin samples, with the Externalizing dimension most strongly reflecting defiant behavior. Symptom domains varied in their measurement properties across levels of Externalizing. This elaborated model of youth Externalizing sets the stage for future investigations of causes and outcomes, and for examining measurement invariance across individuals of diverse backgrounds.

articles_hidden.title: Crowdstorming You Can Trust? Assessing the Reliability of Crowdsourced Ideation and Prioritization
articles_hidden.authors: Younes JEDDI; Maurice Balick; Emile Servan-Schreiber
articles_hidden.abstract: Asking crowds of stakeholders to generate and prioritize ideas has become commonplace, from citizen assemblies to corporate open-innovation challenges. Although the reliability of the results of such consultations is taken for granted, their consistency across independent groups has received little empirical attention, largely because such processes are typically one-off events that cannot easily be repeated. In this exploratory study, we introduce the concept of parallel-crowds reliability, the consistency of outcomes when the same collective intelligence process is applied to the same problem by different but demographically equivalent crowds, and we provide an initial empirical test of it. Two separate but equivalent groups of MBA students in the same course were asked to independently propose and prioritize ideas to improve their MBA program, with the same decision-maker curating and selecting winning ideas in both groups. We assess reliability at three successive stages using semantic similarity measures based on two independent embedding models. We find that the two groups independently proposed semantically similar ideas, with convergence concentrated among valuable ideas and divergence among poor ones. They also prioritized similar ideas similarly, though this correspondence was concentrated among the ideas they judged most valuable, enabling the decision maker to select similar sets of winning ideas. Given the single-domain design, we frame these results as an initial evidence base for future investigations.

articles_hidden.title: Cannabis Use and Binge Eating in Emerging Adults: High Prevalence and High Burden Across Ten Years of the Healthy Minds Study
articles_hidden.authors: Elizabeth Webb Lampe; Lingxiao Liu; Nicholas C. Jacobson
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Existing evidence on co-occurring binge eating and cannabis use is preliminary, and it is unclear how common the combination is or how much burden it carries. We examined both questions among college students, who are high risk for both behaviors.

Method: We pooled ten annual cohorts (2015–16 to 2024–25) of the Healthy Minds Study (577,962 students, 807 campus-year clusters). Eating pathology was measured with the SCOFF loss-of-control item. A subsample of 17,114 students also completed the Eating Disorder Examination Questionnaire (EDE-Q). Estimates were weighted for non-response and clustered by campus.

Results: Across cohorts, loss of control over eating was reported by 39.0% of past-30-day cannabis users and 30.7% of non-users (adjusted OR = 1.43, p < .001). Severe SCOFF screening (score of 4 or higher) rose from 3.5% in non-users to 7.1% in near-daily users (adjusted OR per step = 1.22, p < .001). Weekly binge eating (EDE-Q) was more common among users (23.4% vs. 15.3%; adjusted OR = 1.68, p < .001). Overall, 8.3% of all students reported both behaviors. Students reporting both had higher odds of 10 out of 11 correlates. Relative excess risk due to the interaction between cannabis use and loss of control over eating was positive for depression, self-injury, suicidal ideation, and academic harm (odds ratio based; p < .001).

Conclusions: Binge eating is common among students who use cannabis and is more severe at higher frequencies of cannabis use. Importantly, co-occurrence carried higher odds of depression, suicidality, self-injury, and academic harm. Thus, these cross-sectional findings underscore the need for dedicated longitudinal research.

articles_hidden.title: Appreciating Ambiguity in Art: The effects of semantic distance and insight confidence on aesthetic appreciation
articles_hidden.authors: Rajat Ravi Rao; manon mulckhuyse; Michiel van Elk; Francesco Walker
articles_hidden.abstract: Previous work in psychology of aesthetics suggests that people tend to appreciate artworks they subjectively perceive as ambiguous. Yet ambiguity of an artwork is typically measured through viewers’ own ratings or qualitative measures which are well suited to within-person questions, but they do not, on their own, describe how much viewers disagree about what a work means. Defining ambiguity as the degree to which an artwork affords multiple interpretations, we introduce a computational, description-based measure that quantifies this multiplicity as the semantic distance between viewers’ descriptions. We complemented this with a metacognitive measure, insight confidence, which captures how confident viewers are in their own interpretations. We examined how these measures relate to aesthetic appreciation, operationalised as interest, emotional intensity, and cognitive affect. In an online study (N = 123), participants viewed artworks for 6 seconds and for each individual artwork either described them, rated their insight confidence and provided cognitive affect ratings, or they provided interest and emotional intensity ratings.  Across artworks, those eliciting more divergent descriptions (greater semantic distance) received lower mean insight confidence. Contrary to preregistered predictions, such artworks also received lower aesthetic appreciation. These results indicate aesthetic appreciation is more strongly related to how certain a viewer is about what they are viewing rather than the degree of ambiguity of an artwork. Methodologically, the approach offers a way to quantify the divergence of open-ended verbal interpretations across viewers, alongside a measure of viewers' confidence in their own interpretation.

articles_hidden.title: Transdiagnostic factors differentially shape choices and reaction times in social evaluative learning
articles_hidden.authors: Aamir Sohail; Aleksandra Magda; Muna Said; Laura Phillips; Yifei Lu; Georgina Reynolds; Alice Comer-Fenn; Jessie Russell; Huafeng Lu; Tally Sims
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background
Learning from feedback provided by others is important for navigating complex social environments. Aberrant processing of such social feedback is implicated in the psychopathology of several mental health disorders including social anxiety and depression. Recent psychiatric research increasingly adopts transdiagnostic approaches that examine mechanisms and constructs cutting across traditional diagnostic categories. 

Methods
Here, we applied reinforcement learning models together with transdiagnostic measures of psychopathology to formally assess social evaluation learning. Human participants (n = 193) completed the Social Evaluation Learning Task, learning whether computer personas ‘liked,’ ‘disliked,’ or were ‘neutral’ toward them. Participants also completed six questionnaires assessing socially relevant psychiatric traits. 

Results
Computational modeling revealed that a model with separate learning parameters for positive and negative feedback best accounted for the learning behavior. Exploratory factor analysis identified three transdiagnostic factors. A factor reflecting social avoidance predicted enhanced learning from negative feedback and a reduced positive learning bias. Socially avoidant individuals with heightened negative learning rates additionally showed faster reaction times specifically in positive social contexts. A second factor linking with emotional insensitivity for others predicted a lower choice accuracy in both positively and negatively valanced conditions and was associated with faster reaction times overall. No significant associations emerged for a third factor reflecting depressive and mood-related symptoms. 

Conclusions
These results demonstrate how transdiagnostic trait dimensions shape social learning mechanisms through specific behavioral and computational processes.

articles_hidden.title: Characterizing Rejection Sensitivity in Autistic Adolescents and Implications for Depression and Anxiety Symptoms
articles_hidden.authors: Elika Parab; Colleen Sbeglia; Vana Matevosian; Pia Hernandez; Jessica Schwartzman
articles_hidden.abstract: Adolescence is a developmental period characterized by increased interest in peer relationships and social inclusion. Rejection sensitivity (RS) – the tendency to anticipate, perceive, and experience heightened emotional responses to rejection – is common in adolescence and linked to internalizing symptoms. However, RS is understudied in autistic adolescents despite their social communication differences, increased risk of peer rejection, and online lived experiences of heightened rejection sensitivity. It is also unknown how RS impacts different mental health symptoms and whether it might contribute to the heightened prevalence of anxiety and depression in autistic youth. In the present study, 106 autistic adolescents (14-17 years old) completed surveys of RS, internalizing symptoms, autistic traits, self-esteem, and peer victimization. Results showed that virtually all autistic adolescents experienced a degree of RS, with higher rates among females and those with higher autistic traits. Hierarchical regression models indicated that Anxious RS predicted social anxiety symptoms above and beyond traditional risk and protective factors, but neither Anxious nor Angry RS predicted depression or generalized anxiety. Findings have implications for risk stratification models and point to potential intervention targets; yet more research is needed to determine the directionality of relationships with rejection sensitivity.

articles_hidden.title: Evaluating Ratings from Large Language Models: A Simulation-Based Workflow
articles_hidden.authors: Tim Angelike; Daniel W. Heck
articles_hidden.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used as research tools to facilitate fast and automated ratings of text features. In psychological studies, they have been used to quantify the degree to which stimulus materials reflect certain psychological constructs. However, the application of LLMs entails a high degree of flexibility regarding prompt design (e.g., instruction details and examples) and model specification (e.g., model family, size, and configuration), which can produce divergent results and threaten the robustness and generalizability of conclusions. To navigate the multiverse of possible choices, we develop a systematic workflow for evaluating the quality of LLM-generated ratings across diverse model and prompt specifications. Motivated by generalizability theory, the workflow distinguishes between construct variance across stimulus items, method variance due to model and prompt choices, and residual variance across repeated iterations. To guide researchers through the planning, execution, and reporting of LLM simulation studies, we adapt the ADEMP (Aims, Data-generating mechanism, Estimands and targets, Methods, Performance measures) framework, originally developed for methodological simulation research. We develop a template supporting two complementary validation strategies: assessing consistency across LLM specifications based on generalizability theory via estimated variance components, and external validation against a benchmark (e.g., human ratings). We illustrate the workflow in a preregistered case study using local, open-weight LLMs which examines the influence of model choice, response format, and prompt examples on the quality of valence and arousal ratings for multi-word expressions.

articles_hidden.title: Introducing ResIN: An Applied Tutorial to the Response-Item-Networks Package for R
articles_hidden.authors: Philip Warncke; Dino Carpentras; Adrian Lueders; Michael Quayle
articles_hidden.abstract: We introduce ResIN, a package for the R programming language designed to estimate, visualize, and analyze Response-Item Networks (ResIN ). ResIN is an increasingly popular method for modeling complex socio-political attitude systems as sparse, spatially interpretable networks. The package simplifies and unifies the underlying workflow while offering a range of convenience features, including network plotting, community detection, psychometric score extraction, bootstrap-based uncertainty estimation, and the export of ResIN objects to other statistical software environments. We provide an overview of the ResIN method, its computational implementation in R, and demonstrate the utility of key package features through an applied replication tutorial based on a recent study by Lüders et al., 2024

articles_hidden.title: Thought for food: Individual differences in how food decisions are made
articles_hidden.authors: Caitlin Lloyd; Zarrar Shehzad; Janet Schebendach; Akram Bakkour; Alice M Xue; Naomi Assaf; Rayman Jiliani; B. Timothy Walsh; Daphna Shohamy; Joanna Steinglass
articles_hidden.abstract: Daily food decisions accumulate to impact physical health, but making choices consistent with longer-term health goals can prove challenging. Prior research has focused predominantly on dampening preferences for highly palatable foods, or exerting self-control, as the mechanism for healthier food choices. Consequently, the range of cognitive strategies for healthy eating, and how they vary with demographic characteristics, remains unclear. Here, a large US sample (N = 1,052) completed an online food rating and choice task, and demographic and eating behavior questionnaires. Participants rated foods across 17 dimensions, which were reduced to three underlying core food attributes by factor analysis: Tastiness, Healthiness, and Umami (capturing food savoriness). All attributes influenced food choices. A multi-attribute drift diffusion model quantified distinct yet latent choice processes, including the deliberation required prior to making a choice. The influence of Tastiness, Healthiness, and Umami on choice varied across the study population. Women, individuals endorsing higher levels of eating restraint, and individuals with lower BMI selected subjectively healthier foods more frequently. Making subjectively healthier choices was not dependent only on engaging self-control. Rather, individuals making subjectively healthier choices perceived subjectively healthier foods as tastier. In addition, individuals endorsing high levels of eating restraint required less deliberation when making choices, suggesting more automatic decision-making. These findings suggest multiple routes to making healthier food choices and question the narrative that food tastiness must be sacrificed to support physical health.

articles_hidden.title: Literacy Skills are Related to Audiovisual Speech Perception in School-Aged Children
articles_hidden.authors: Shakhlo Nematova; Sarah Akkad; Henry Brice; Kaja Kinga Jasińska
articles_hidden.abstract: Does learning to read influence children’s audiovisual (AV) speech perception? This study aimed to answer this question by delving into whether the process of learning to read in Uzbek, a language with a transparent orthography, influences the sensitivity to AV speech cues (i.e., mouth movements corresponding to phonetic/lexical information). Furthermore, the study examined the mediating role of phonological awareness (PA) skills in potentially linking reading and AV speech sensitivity. 283 pre-readers (age=5-6 years) and readers (age=7-10 years) in Tashkent, Uzbekistan completed PA, AV speech perception, and reading assessments. Overall, better reading skills predicted increased sensitivity to AV speech cues. These findings suggest that there is a potential shared mechanism between reading and AV speech perception. However, in the case of languages with transparent orthographies, this shared mechanism does not seem to be significantly mediated by phonological awareness skills of children.

articles_hidden.title: Daily Diary Study of Sexual and Gender Minority Emerging Adults’ Stressors:  Codesign and Preliminary Findings
articles_hidden.authors: Noah J French; Margaret Atkinson-Barnes; Tanvi Lakhtakia; Emma C. Wolfe; Md. Sabbir Ahmed; Laura Barnes; Bethany Teachman
articles_hidden.abstract: Emerging adulthood involves impactful developmental milestones for sexual and gender minority (SGM) individuals and is a critical period for understanding stress processes. Most existing SGM stress research is cross-sectional, with relatively little known about the everyday experiences that may confer mental health risk or resilience for SGM emerging adults. N = 104 SGM emerging adults (age: M = 20.21 years, SD = 1.92 years; 76% assigned female at birth; 35% gender minority; 53% Bisexual+; 55% White) were recruited to codesign (Phases 1-2) or complete for 14 days (Phase 3) a daily diary measure of identity-related and non-identity-related stressors and positive identity-related experiences. Phase 1 participants (n = 8) completed qualitative interviews and provided feedback on an initial draft measure. Phase 2 participants (n = 6) piloted a revised measure for seven days before providing feedback in qualitative interviews. Phase 3 participants (n = 90) completed the final measure for 14 days. Qualitative data from Phases 1-2 were analyzed using the immersion-crystallization framework, and descriptive statistics were computed for Phase 3 quantitative data. In Phases 1-2, participants emphasized the need to capture chronic stressors and stress tied to recent sociopolitical events in the U.S. In Phase 3, non-identity-related stressors were more frequent than identity-related stressors, proximal identity-related stressors were more frequent than distal identity-related stressors, and negative intersectional experiences and positive identity-related experiences were both common. Results highlight the importance of involving participants with lived experiences in all stages of survey design.

articles_hidden.title: Patterns of Reactivity in Misophonia: Profiles of Behavioral and Self-Reported Symptoms
articles_hidden.authors: Nico Remmert; Mercedes Woolley; Marta Siepsiak; Michael Twohig; Steffi Pohl
articles_hidden.abstract: Individuals with misophonia experience intense affective reactions to trigger sounds and often cope through avoidance. Avoidance may be anticipatory (preventing exposure) or reactive (escaping exposure), but individual patterns remain poorly understood. In a sample of individuals with misophonia (N = 370), we used Gaussian mixture modeling to identify profiles based on anticipatory avoidance, reactive escape, and emotional responses. We compared profiles derived from behavioral assessments and self-reports and examined their associations with clinical outcomes. Behavioral data revealed three qualitatively distinct profiles: high affective reactivity, anticipatory-dominant reactivity, and reactive-dominant reactivity. Self-reports instead yielded four profiles that mainly reflected severity differences. Agreement between methods was modest, suggesting that they capture partly different aspects of misophonic responding. Behavioral profiles also differed in clinically relevant outcomes. These findings highlight the value of behavioral assessment for identifying distinct response styles and advancing understanding of misophonia beyond symptom severity.

articles_hidden.title: Self-Reported Precipitants of Psychosis, Mania, and Depression: An AI-Assisted Analysis of Reddit
articles_hidden.authors: Ari Brouwer; Charles L Raison
articles_hidden.abstract: We examined self-reported precipitants of mania, psychosis, and depression on Reddit using AI-assisted code development and automated coding, with blinded human validation. Analyses compared precipitants of mania (n = 337), psychosis (n = 339), and depression (n = 252). Generic stress and sleep disruption were common to mania and psychosis but rare in depression. Cannabis and trauma/abuse/assault were more frequently reported for psychosis, while antidepressants and positive activation/reward were more frequently reported for mania, and self-evaluative thought patterns and social isolation/rejection for depression. Automated and human coding showed strong agreement (κ = 0.82), supporting the feasibility of AI-assisted analysis of perceived psychiatric precipitants.

articles_hidden.title: Are males victims of intimate partner violence in Greece? Prevalence of the phenomenon and implications for mental health
articles_hidden.authors: Panagiota Peleka; Aglaia Katsiroumpa; Ioannis Moisoglou; Angeliki Triantafillaki; Olympia Konstantakopoulou; Anastasia Tsalouka; Maria Tsiachri; Antigoni Kolisiati; Petros Galanis
articles_hidden.abstract: OBJECTIVE To investigate the association between intimate partner violence (IPV) and mental health among males in a Greek population. METHODS A cross-sectional online survey was conducted in Greece in July 2026. IPV among males was assessed using the Woman Abuse Screening Tool (WAST), while the lifetime prevalence of physical, psychological/emotional, and sexual abuse was evaluated through three dichotomous self-report items (yes/no). Anxiety-like and depressive-like symptoms were measured using the Patient Health Questionnaire-4 (PHQ-4). Sleep quality was assessed with the Single-Item Sleep Quality Scale (SQS), self-esteem with the Single-Item Self-Esteem Scale (SISE), loneliness with the UCLA 3-Item Loneliness Scale (UCLA-LS-3), and life satisfaction with the Satisfaction with Life Scale (SWLS). To account for the potential influence of demographic characteristics, multivariable linear regression analyses were performed with adjustment for relevant demographic confounding variables. RESULTS In the adjusted model, higher levels of males’ abuse (WAST score) were significantly associated with higher levels of anxiety-like symptoms. Additionally, levels of anxiety-like symptoms were higher among males that have experienced physical abuse, and psychological/emotional abuse through their lives. Multivariable model found that higher levels of males’ abuse (WAST score) were significantly associated with higher levels of depressive-like symptoms. Additionally, levels of depressive-like symptoms were higher among males that have experienced physical abuse, and psychological/emotional abuse through their lives. Sleep quality was worse among males that have experienced physical abuse, and psychological/emotional abuse through their lives. Higher levels of males’ abuse (WAST score) were significantly associated with lower levels of self-esteem. Additionally, levels of self-esteem were lower among males that have experienced physical abuse through their lives. Higher levels of males’ abuse (WAST score) were significantly associated with higher levels of loneliness. Higher levels of males’ abuse (WAST score) were significantly associated with lower levels of life satisfaction. Additionally, levels of life satisfaction were lower among males that have experienced psychological/emotional abuse through their lives. CONCLUSIONS IPV was significantly associated with poorer mental health and psychosocial well-being among males in Greece. Greater exposure to abusive behaviors was associated with higher levels of anxiety-like symptoms, depressive-like symptoms, and loneliness, as well as poorer sleep quality, lower self-esteem, and reduced life satisfaction. These findings highlight the substantial psychological burden associated with IPV and underscore its detrimental impact on multiple dimensions of mental health and well-being among male victims.

articles_hidden.title: The Museum as a Spatial System: Bodily Movement, Visual Comparison and Memory in Art Viewing
articles_hidden.authors: Anna Miscenà; Xingyu Long; Carola Korhummel; Zoya Dare; Dijana Popovic; Corinna Kühnapfel; Jörg Helmut Mühlhans; Raphael Rosenberg
articles_hidden.abstract: Art viewing in museums inherently relies on physical movement through galleries. While research has begun to examine movement in art perception, it has focused mainly on abstract paintings and small-scale case studies. We investigated how bodily movement, gaze behaviour and memory interact with a mobile-eye-tracking study in Vienna's Leopold Museum (145 visitors viewing 66 paintings across six rooms). The results show that a) although visitors increased their viewing distance for larger paintings, they did not maintain a constant visual angle, b) visitors repositioned themselves mainly laterally in front of paintings, and c) they frequently compared neighbouring artworks by repeating gazes between paintings. Longer viewing times and repeated returns to a painting were associated with better subsequent memory. These findings suggest that the museum's "white cube" is not a neutral backdrop for independent encounters but a spatially organised environment that shapes horizontal exploration as well as visual comparison between adjacent works.

articles_hidden.title: Simulation-based cutoffs for conditional item fit in Rasch models: iterations, multiplicity correction, and decision stability
articles_hidden.authors: Magnus Johansson
articles_hidden.abstract:
Simulation-based cutoff values for conditional item fit can be estimated by parametric bootstrapping
and reported as an interval of a chosen width. Johansson (2025) recommended this
over rule-of-thumb critical values and gave iteration guidance based on detection rates and
conditioned on sample size, without an account of the error rate that the interval width controls.
This paper re-examines iterations and width against the familywise error rate (FWER),
and compares FWER and false discovery rate control. Seven simulation studies vary item count
and the targeting of misfitting items, with both dichotomous and polytomous conditions.

The interval width is shown to be the error rate parameter of the procedure, setting the
FWER jointly with the number of items. Bootstrap p-values with a Westfall-Young FWER
correction target that error rate directly, detect more misfit than a width-matched interval,
and are calibrated from 400 iterations, with fewer false positives than Benjamini-Hochberg.
Outfit was consistently less powerful than infit, confirming earlier dichotomous findings and
extending them to polytomous items.

Updated recommendations include flagging items on the Westfall-Young FWER corrected
p-value, using at least 400 iterations and 1000 to 2000 for a final analysis, and reporting the
interval as a descriptive band at width .95. The described methods are available in the R
package easyRasch2 and the jamovi module easyRasch2jmv.

articles_hidden.title: More Visibility for Diversity? A Systematic Review of LGBTQ+ Representation in Educational Psychology Journals
articles_hidden.authors: Valentin Emslander; Oliver Adam Kluge; Christoph Niepel
articles_hidden.abstract: Students identifying as lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, or otherwise non-heterosexual or non-cisgender (LGBTQ+) are increasingly represented. However, they still face additional challenges in educational settings, so Educational Psychology needs to research these issues. In this preregistered systematic scientometric literature review, we investigate (a) the extent of LGBTQ+ centered research in Educational Psychology journals, (b) common themes and trends, and discuss systematic gaps for future research. After searching all 41,992 articles on ERIC, published in the most impactful (Q1 and Q2) Educational Psychology journals, we combined scientometric-quantitative and qualitative methods to review 68 eligible articles. We found a surge in publications from 2000 onward, driven by special issues. For almost half of these high-impact journals, we found no published articles on LGBTQ+ issues on ERIC; most publish only a few per thousand, even though this topic falls within their scope. Most often, these articles were empirical, correlational, and US-based, with inconsistent measures of LGBTQ+ identities. Through qualitative thematic analysis, we identified seven research themes and highlighted pertinent research gaps. To strengthen the evidence base in the field, future research should conduct rigorous longitudinal and intervention studies with culturally diverse samples and adhere to open science standards.

articles_hidden.title: Dynamic Structural Equation Modeling: A Tutorial Using Stan
articles_hidden.authors: Jean-Paul Snijder-Steinhilber; Anna-Lena Schubert; Andreas B. Neubauer
articles_hidden.abstract: Dynamic structural equation modeling (DSEM) has become a central tool for analyzing intensive longitudinal data, such as data from ecological momentary assessment and daily diary studies. In practice, DSEM is almost exclusively estimated in Mplus, a commercial, closed-source program, while packages built on the open-source probabilistic programming language Stan offer only a fixed selection of models. This tutorial shows applied researchers how to implement DSEM directly in Stan. Starting from a bivariate multilevel cross-lagged model with random effects, we build the model in three steps: a minimal working version, a non-centered reparameterization that resolves the convergence problems of the first version, and an extension that treats missing observations as parameters to be estimated. Along the way, we explain how to read Stan's convergence and sampler diagnostics, how to inspect the results visually, and how to report a Bayesian DSEM. On simulated data with known parameter values, the Stan implementation recovers the true values and closely reproduces the estimates of Mplus and of the R package mlts. We then demonstrate the flexibility of working in Stan with two extensions that require only local changes to the code: residual DSEM, and a binary within-person predictor, illustrated with data from a micro-randomized mindfulness intervention. All code is openly available and written to be adapted to new models. Working directly in Stan requires more initial effort than Mplus, but it makes every modeling decision transparent and extensible, and it lets researchers fit the model their research question calls for.

articles_hidden.title: The FlexER-Scale: A new Self-report Measure of Individual Differences in Emotion Regulation Flexibility
articles_hidden.authors: Anne Gärtner; Christoph Scheffel; Timo Schweikert; Denise Dörfel
articles_hidden.abstract: Previous research on emotion regulation (ER) has primarily focused on individual strategies and their association with well-being and psychopathology. Recent frameworks emphasize a context-sensitive, goal-dependent approach, defining ER flexibility as the ability to adaptively adjust ER strategies based on contextual demands and personal goals. Despite growing evidence for its relevance, a concise self-report measure designed to capture trait-level, strategy-independent ER flexibility has been lacking. To address this gap, we developed the Flexible Emotion Regulation Scale (FlexER-Scale) and validated it using data from four independent samples (N = 1,019). Exploratory factor analysis (EFA) and confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) in an independent sample examined the scale’s structure; criterion validity was assessed via correlations with the WHO-5 Well-Being Index and the Emotion Regulation Questionnaire (ERQ). The final 10-item FlexER-Scale demonstrated good psychometric properties, including satisfactory item discrimination and high internal consistency (α = .85). EFA suggested a two-factor structure differentiating hedonic and contra-hedonic ER flexibility, which was supported by CFA. The FlexER-Scale showed a significant positive correlation with psychological well-being, driven by the hedonic factor. Small but significant correlations with habitual reappraisal and suppression use provided initial evidence for discriminant validity. The FlexER-Scale is a promising tool for assessing ER flexibility, offering a concise alternative to existing measures by capturing adaptive regulatory variability without relying on predefined strategies. Future research should examine its construct validity, longitudinal stability, and predictive validity. Given that the validation was based on predominantly student samples from a German-speaking context, broader generalizability remains to be established.

articles_hidden.title: Cognitive Model Organism: The Unboxing of Thinking Process
articles_hidden.authors: Yuncheng Jia; Bo Qin; Anuchit Phanumartwiwath
articles_hidden.abstract: We establish the Hortus Regis Alti (HRA) Experimental and Observational Protocol for studying a frozen language model as a cognitive model organism. The preparation combines controlled input perturbations, complete native-token preservation, deterministic symbolic probes, contextual process coding, and explicit failure screening. One DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B implementation with INT8 linear layers and BF16 elsewhere produced 176 archived trajectories across four observation configurations of one Bayesian decision problem, containing 2,205,963 generated tokens. Eight baseline pairs regenerated identical overlapping prefixes across 93,016 token positions. Three empirical demonstrations organize the study. Symbolic closure separated from execution termination, including renewed processing after a closure marker. Aggregate consumption separated from item-specific response paths: 36 of 40 four-level item series changed direction. Correct local computation separated from maintenance of task representation: an auxiliary result could be calculated correctly and subsequently rebound as an operand. Complete contextual reading localized 1,926 evidence anchors, including successful repairs and recurrent failures. Measurement checks further showed that a short window could classify a long exact cycle as highly diverse. These findings motivate testable hypotheses of representational control competition, training-register capture, and content-specific effects of symbolic continuation. The contribution is a process-oriented experimental preparation, a reproducible trajectory collection, and a quality-control procedure that connects observable symbolic events to discriminating intervention sites. Precision specifications identify the model strain, execution conditions, measurement units, semantic coding decisions, and regeneration range supporting these claims.

articles_hidden.title: Using a Foreign Language Does Not Make the Art More Profound - Familiarity Does
articles_hidden.authors: Wojciech Milczarski; Anna Borkowska; Susanne Brouwer; Michal Bialek
articles_hidden.abstract: This study investigated whether using a foreign language affects aesthetic judgments of art. Across three experiments (N=345), Polish-English and Dutch-English bilinguals rated songs and paintings on profoundness, liking, recommendation, and familiarity. Participants completed the study in either their native or foreign language, allowing us to examine the Foreign Language Effect on judgments of both language-rich content (songs with lyrics) and language-poor content (paintings). Contrary to theoretical predictions based on reduced emotional engagement and impaired metacognition in foreign languages, presentation language did not significantly affect any ratings. Instead, two factors consistently predicted profoundness judgments: familiarity and medium. Participants rated familiar artworks as more profound regardless of language condition, and music received higher profoundness ratings than paintings across all experiments. These findings suggest that aesthetic perception is primarily driven by prior exposure and medium-specific characteristics rather than the language in which art is encountered, challenging assumptions about linguistic effects on aesthetic judgments.

articles_hidden.title: Workplace Greenery and Work Engagement Among Live-In Shiftworkers: A Conceptual Replication of Popov et al. (2023)
articles_hidden.authors: Caroline Isabelle Ekeberg; Kristin Kloster; Peder Mortvedt Isager
articles_hidden.abstract: This study presents a conceptual replication of @popov2023 (Study 2), examining whether workplace greenery is associated with work engagement in a novel occupational and seasonal context. Ninety-four live-in shiftworkers (55.3% women) employed in Norwegian assisted living facilities for adults with intellectual disabilities and/or autism spectrum disorders completed an online survey during autumn 2024. Work engagement was measured with the Utrecht Work Engagement Scale, and three forms of workplace greenery were assessed: window views of nature, access to outdoor natural environments, and the presence of indoor plants. Analyses of covariance, controlling for job demands and appreciation of natural beauty, largely replicated the original pattern of results. Access to outdoor natural environments—both during breaks and while accompanying service users—was significantly associated with higher work engagement, whereas window views and indoor plants showed no reliable effects. Gender did not consistently moderate these associations. The findings provide evidence that the association between outdoor nature exposure and work engagement may extend to live-in shiftworkers and an autumn context.

articles_hidden.title: Is it Difficult to be a People-Pleaser? An Item Response-Theoretical Examination of the People Pleasing Scale
articles_hidden.authors: Christian Blötner; Johanna Werner
articles_hidden.abstract: The phenomenon of people-pleasing (i.e., the tendency to sacrifice one’s own needs and obligations to help others) has recently attracted considerable attention in popular psychology. Empirical research has been devoted only recently to the development and validation of suitable measurement tools such as the People Pleasing Scale (Blötner, 2026; https://doi.org/10.1007/s12144-026-09519-2). The measure provides desirable psychometric properties from the perspective of Classical Test Theory, but in this framework, several statistical assumptions about item and scale characteristics remain untested. To address this gap, we subjected the People Pleasing Scale to item response-theoretical examinations as per the polytomous Graded Response Model (N = 2,538). The three-factor solution (Responsibility, Neglect of Own Needs, and Others’ Expectations) elicited sufficient model and item fit and predominant support for the assumption of local independence. Its three subscales provided favorable item discrimination and threshold parameters indicating that endorsement of the highest response categories requires only moderately elevated levels of people-pleasing. Seven of the 10 items provided information across comparatively broad regions of the latent trait continuum, albeit with lower peak information. These findings illustrate candidate items for future scale shortening without substantial loss of measurement precision.

articles_hidden.title: Eat your vegetables: Exploring food learning cues in 12-month-old infants
articles_hidden.authors: Camille Rioux; Karola Schlegelmilch; Annie E. Wertz
articles_hidden.abstract: Food learning in early life largely relies on social learning. Previous research has shown that infants learn something is edible when they directly observe someone else eating it. However, the role of other forms of food-related social information remains largely unknown. Food processing actions (e.g., chopping, mashing) are essential components of human food behaviors and a ubiquitous part of infants’ everyday lives. Here we examined whether infants (i) differentially attend to eating and food processing actions compared to control actions and (ii) learn that novel foods are edible after observing eating and food processing actions performed with them. We tested 12-month-olds’ responses to three different actions: eating, food processing, and a control action (touch). First, we showed infants side-by-side videos of an adult performing two different actions with novel foods across three between-subjects conditions and measured their gaze and pupil dilation with an eye-tracker. Then, we offered infants the novel foods shown in the videos and measured their choices and eating behaviors. Our eye-tracking results indicate that infants differentially attend to eating and food processing actions relative to the control action, and show increased pupil dilation for the control action relative to the two actions that may indicate edibility (eating and cutting). When asked to choose which novel food they could eat, infants chose the novel food they saw an actor eat, but only when that eating action was paired with the control action. These findings help identify important mechanisms that increase acceptance of healthy foods early in life.

articles_hidden.title: Working Memory Development: Cross-Sectional and Longitudinal Analyses of Primary School Children in an Adaptive Learning Environment
articles_hidden.authors: Şeyma Nur Ertekin; Abe Dirk Hofman; Evie Vergauwe; Julia M. Haaf
articles_hidden.abstract: The present study investigated the spatial working memory (WM) ability and its developmental change, utilizing large-scale cross-sectional and longitudinal data from an adaptive learning environment. Approximately 16% of Dutch primary school children participated in a spatial serial recall task between 2019 and 2025, providing dense, continuous measurements of the same children in their regular educational environment. Cross-sectional analyses demonstrated the increase of working memory capacity between the ages of six and twelve on average by one item. However, the spatial complexity of the lists affected this capacity increase. Moreover, longitudinal analyses of accuracy demonstrated WM ability maturation over time, yet there was no impact of practicing the task. Furthermore, significant individual differences were observed among children. Future studies should focus on a better assessment of spatial complexity and the underlying sources for individual differences in WM development.

articles_hidden.title: Mapping the Body in the Brain with the Mind
articles_hidden.authors: Alexander M Puckett; Ashley York; Saskia Bollmann; Ross Cunnington
articles_hidden.abstract: Using a magnet and a mind, we revealed the brain’s somatotopic organization without touching the body. Fingertip representations were first mapped using vibrotactile stimulation at 7T, then again by directing attention across the fingers under constant vibration. Finally, attention was directed to the fingertips and facial regions using only auditory cues, without any external tactile stimulation. Prior training in a sensory-restricted float tank subjectively sharpened attentional precision and bodily awareness. Remarkably, somatotopic maps emerged in the absence of external tactile stimulation – showing that structured attention alone can reveal the brain’s somatotopic organization.

articles_hidden.title: Developing Effective GenAI Users: The Missing Motivational System and Why It Matters for Equity
articles_hidden.authors: Kali Trzesniewski; Sarah J Gripshover; Allison Master
articles_hidden.abstract: Research on Generative AI (GenAI) in education has largely focused on how much students use it and its impact on learning. This framing overlooks the motivational processes driving students’ choices. We propose broadening research to include the study of what cultures, contexts, and learning experiences give students the knowledge, skills, beliefs, and motivation to become effective GenAI users. We define effective GenAI use and propose a motivational model of how learning environments and students' perceptions of them shape their goals and GenAI engagement choices, with attention to educational inequities that may emerge.

articles_hidden.title: Enhancing measurement in adaptive learning systems: How much can we gain from response times?
articles_hidden.authors: Maria Bolsinova; Jesper Tijmstra; Matthieu J. S. Brinkhuis; Abe Dirk Hofman; Bence Gergely
articles_hidden.abstract:
Obtaining accurate measures of changing abilities is essential for online adaptive learning systems (ALS) to provide learners with instructional material and practice items at the appropriate level. 
Despite the large data volume in ALS, focusing on a single individual at a specific moment yields limited data, reducing measurement precision. To improve quality of measurement in ALS, it has been proposed to incorporate response time (RT) data into measurement (Klinkenberg et al., 2011). Using data from an ALS for primary school mathematics Math Garden (Straatemeier, 2014), we compare different models that incorporate RTs and can be used for ability tracking with each other and with the benchmark Rasch model, in which ability is measured based only on the accuracy of the responses. We also contrast these empirical findings with simulation results that match the empirical setup but where the generating model matches the way in which RTs are incorporated into measurement, to study what can be gained under ideal circumstances. Our results show that while theoretical gains are large, in the studied empirical setting RTs at best provide a modest improvement that was not fully consistent across domains and depended on the reward system implemented in the ALS. Implications of the results for the choice of the measurement model in ALS are discussed.

articles_hidden.title: Covert consciousness is not cognitive motor dissociation and the vegetative state is not a state of mind
articles_hidden.authors: Martin M Monti; Caroline Schnakers; Nicholas D. Schiff; Yelena G Bodien
articles_hidden.abstract: The discovery of covert consciousness (CC) and cognitive motor dissociation (CMD) has revealed a conceptual inconsistency at the heart of disorders of consciousness (DoC) nosology. Advanced neuroimaging and electrophysiological studies have demonstrated that behavioral unresponsiveness does not necessarily imply the absence of consciousness or cognitive capacity, yet contemporary diagnostic categories continue equating unresponsiveness with unconsciousness. This equivalence is embedded throughout DoC nomenclature, where behavioral syndromes such as the vegetative state (VS) and minimally conscious state (MCS) are defined by what patients are inferred to experience (i.e., their state of mind) but operationalized on the basis of what they are observed to do (or not do). We argue that this category error now impedes the translation of over two decades of scientific advances into a coherent clinical framework. First, it has fostered the widespread but incorrect conflation of covert consciousness (CC) and cognitive motor dissociation (CMD), despite the fact that the two concepts identify different patient populations and may carry distinct implications for diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment. Second, it renders contemporary DoC nosology incapable of coherently incorporating modern neuroimaging and electrophysiological findings. Because the absence of consciousness is an entrenched, definitional component of the VS, its behavioral phenotype cannot be reconciled with covert neurophysiological phenotypes such as CC and CMD. As a result, current nomenclature impedes the development of a phenotype-endotype framework in which bedside behavioral classifications are complemented by biologically informed categories derived from advanced neuroimaging and electrophysiological assessments. We trace the origins of this problem to a historical shift whereby the definitions of VS and MCS evolved from descriptions of observable behavior into claims about a patient’s mental state. Disentangling responsiveness from consciousness, we argue, is essential if the field is to incorporate contemporary evidence and develop a coherent, biologically informed nosology of DoC, which, in our view, is best pursued within a phenotype-endotype framework.

articles_hidden.title: The Role of Menstrual Cycle Phase in PTSD: A Scoping Review of Symptom Expression, Neuropsychology and Psychotherapy Response in Women
articles_hidden.authors: Ciara Treacy; Mia Schaumberg; Katherine Moore; Ella Liow; Sophie Andrews; Bronwyn Graham; Alain Brunet
articles_hidden.abstract: Women are diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) at twice the rate of men, a disparity only partly explained by trauma exposure differences. Sex-specific biological factors, particularly cyclic fluctuations in estradiol and progesterone, have been associated with PTSD symptoms/related neuropsychological processes in healthy/trauma exposed women; however, the extent and clinical translation of this literature (if any) remain unclear in PTSD populations. This review aimed to map evidence examining associations between ovarian hormones/menstrual cycle phase and PTSD symptoms and/or related neuropsychological processes (e.g., extinction learning) in women with PTSD (Aim1), and/or associations with psychotherapy outcomes in PTSD/related anxiety disorders (Aim2). A systematic search for peer-reviewed, empirical studies involving adult females was conducted across 6 databases, in accordance with PRISMA-ScR and JBI guidelines. From 2,464 results, 12 studies were included. Five studies addressed Aim 1 and seven addressed Aim 2. Hormonal operationalization was inconsistent, including continuous assays (n=5), menstrual cycle phase comparisons (n=3), and/or median split/other groupings (n=6), with estradiol most frequently measured. For Aim 1, PTSD symptom findings were inconsistent and inconclusive (n=3), whereas lower estradiol was more consistently associated with impaired fear extinction and habituation (n=2). For Aim 2, findings in anxiety-related disorders were mixed, with no study examining ovarian hormone status in psychotherapy outcomes for women with PTSD. Overall, evidence remains sparse, heterogeneous and largely cross-sectional. Findings do not yet support firm conclusions regarding ovarian hormone–PTSD symptom/neuropsychological interactions but highlight key research gaps and future directions to better understand these relationships and inform personalized PTSD treatments for women.

articles_hidden.title: Video games in cognitive event-related EEG research: A scoping review
articles_hidden.authors: Belinda Fleischmann; Sean Mulready; Dirk Ostwald
articles_hidden.abstract: Event-related EEG research has traditionally relied on controlled laboratory tasks with limited ecological validity. Video games offer a middle ground between laboratory and real-world settings, combining intuitive interaction with experimental control. This scoping review, reported according to PRISMA-ScR, characterizes video game paradigms used in event-related EEG research and relates their findings to canonical laboratory effects. Database and supplementary searches identified 29 studies using 26 paradigms. Most paradigms used custom-built games and required visuomotor navigation or targeting within continuous gameplay, and most analyses were time-locked to feedback events such as hits or collisions. Findings showed selective convergence with laboratory effects, particularly for P3-like positivities sensitive to event probability, outcome magnitude, and player relevance, and for movement-related activity. Evidence for error- and feedback-related components was more limited, while early sensory responses were rarely examined. We discuss emerging patterns in the use of video games as event-related EEG paradigms, the correspondence between game-elicited and laboratory EEG effects, and the methodological challenges of studying event-related activity during gameplay. In sum, this synthesis aims to guide the selection and design of game paradigms, inform expectations about neural responses during gameplay, and support their interpretation in light of established laboratory findings in future research in this emerging field.

articles_hidden.title: Toward Sensory Accounts of Autistic Masking: A Perspective
articles_hidden.authors: Rebecca Poulsen; Melanie Heyworth; Timothy Chan; Diana Weiting Tan
articles_hidden.abstract: Autistic masking has typically been understood as the suppression of natural Autistic traits within neuronormative social contexts. However, social interactions are inherently embedded within broader sensory environments, highlighting the need to consider how sensory experiences shape masking processes. Although sensory experiences have been recognized within existing masking research, the sensory dimensions of masking remain comparatively underexplored. In this perspective, we examine sensory masking as an interrelated dimension of broader Autistic masking processes, defined as the conscious or subconscious suppression, inhibition, or override of sensory responses to meet environmental or social expectations. Drawing on recent research and our own lived experience, we describe how these sensory dimensions may emerge developmentally, often as a learned adaptation to unsafe or invalidating experiences. We then consider the cumulative effects of sustained sensory masking. While sensory masking may serve a functional purpose, its chronic and persistent engagement may contribute to burnout and negatively impact well-being and mental health, particularly in the context of prolonged exposure to sensory aversive environments. We also distinguish these sensory dimensions from related processes of sensory self-regulation and sensory unmasking, which involve supporting regulation and reclaiming autonomy through safe sensory self-expression. We conclude by outlining constructive approaches that support sensory safety, self-regulation, and well-being, and propose future research directions to explore the mechanisms, impacts, and potential supports associated with the sensory dimensions of masking.

articles_hidden.title: Computationally efficient interval estimation for the 1-1-1 multilevel mediation analysis model in R: A replication of Bauer, Preacher, and Gil (2006)
articles_hidden.authors: Carl F. Falk; Elizabeth Savchenko
articles_hidden.abstract: Bauer, Preacher, and Gil (2006) developed a popular estimation approach for the 1-1-1 multilevel mediation analysis model, using simulations to evaluate the performance of two computationally efficient ways to obtain intervals for the indirect effect. While the model can be estimated in a variety of software packages, support in R lags behind as the original approaches to interval estimation were demonstrated using commercial software. Recent research with R instead has only demonstrated interval estimation with more computationally intensive methods. Meanwhile, other recent work has focused attention towards how Monte Carlo simulation studies are conducted and reported, highlighting the importance of replicating previous findings. Our goals in this manuscript are twofold. First, we show how to implement the original computationally efficient interval estimation methods for the 1-1-1 multilevel mediation analysis model in R. We do so by using the Delta method to obtain elements of the asymptotic covariance matrix among model parameters necessary for these approaches. Second, in a pre-registered study, we evaluate our implementation by attempting to partially replicate the original simulation study by Bauer et al. (2006). In general, our results indicate that our implementation is operating as expected as Type I error rates and coverage were acceptable when assumptions were met. Furthermore, though we observed higher convergence rates, the major findings from Bauer et al. (2006) were replicated. We hope that extensions to this work will help lead to more advanced multilevel mediation analysis models being readily available to applied researchers.

articles_hidden.title: Learning and Using Value Maps in Multi-Dimensional Choice
articles_hidden.authors: Ata Baris Karagoz; Akram Bakkour
articles_hidden.abstract:
When making choices between multi-dimensional options, people draw upon knowledge
of the options’ various properties to make a decision. While much work has probed how
individuals make decisions in these modes, less is known of how learned value maps can
be flexibly composed to support novel decisions. Here we taught participants three separate
perceptual-to-value mappings, each dividing a continuous perceptual dimension into five value
categories. We then had them choose between composite options never encountered during
learning while a mouse-contingent display forced serial information sampling. How the learned
map was read during choice varied widely across people, from fully metric reads (e.g. how
much better) to purely ordinal ones (e.g. which is ahead). We find that ordinal comparison is
not simply a degraded version of the same metric. Instead, participants mix between ordinal
and metric reads. How well each dimension was learned set its weight, while how strongly
learning accuracy depended on the separation between categories lowered both the weights
and the metric share of the read. Both the readout and weights left separable signatures in
information search. Learned value maps are thus composed and then read out to guide choice.

articles_hidden.title: Delusion-like content emerges from common-cause inference over semantically disparate observations
articles_hidden.authors: Matthew Schafer; Emmett M. Larsen; Kiyohito Iigaya; Guillermo Horga
articles_hidden.abstract: Delusions are beliefs with extraordinary content, yet computational accounts of delusions have not explained how this content arises. We propose that extraordinary content emerges when an ordinary mechanism, common-cause inference, is applied to semantically disparate observations. We tested this with large language models (LLMs) by systematically manipulating semantic disparity between observations. Single causes inferred by these models from ordinary observations generally resembled true causes, yet became increasingly delusion-like as observations became more disparate. Observation disparity predicted delusionality, and this relationship could be explained geometrically via semantic analogues of common-cause properties. We further tested this idea in a large corpus of real-world delusions. In cases documenting pre-delusional observations, subsequent delusional beliefs were consistent with what LLMs would infer and exhibited corresponding common-cause properties. Together, our findings identify a computational route through which extraordinary delusion-like content can emerge from ordinary causal inference, and demonstrate its relevance to clinical delusions.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond individual features: Identifying computational principles in perceiving visual beauty
articles_hidden.authors: Mustafa Alperen Ekinci; Philipp Flieger; Daniel Kaiser
articles_hidden.abstract: Prior research in empirical aesthetics has related beauty to visual features like curvature, color, or shape. Although these feature-based accounts have identified reliable visual correlates of beauty, the literature on feature preferences is highly fragmented, with individual features studied for individual stimulus domains. Here, we argue that making further progress hinges on complementing feature-based approaches with approaches aimed at distilling computational principles that underlie the perception of beauty. Recent advances in computational neuroscience can drive this new line of research by linking visual beauty to the coding of visual information in artificial neural networks and the biological brain. We highlight two examples of how this approach has identified overarching computational principles. First, metabolic processing costs, both in artificial and biological vision, are inversely related to perceived beauty, suggesting that beauty may reflect energy-efficient, fluent visual coding. Second, integrative processing in artificial and biological vision captures the efficient spatial representation of image elements across space and predicts beauty ratings. Synthesizing these findings, we derive a neuro-computational framework for assessing computational principles in the perception of beauty, which uses artificial neural networks for exploration at scale and then validates candidate principles using human behavior and brain data. We discuss candidate principles that could be explored using this approach, like spatiotemporal predictability, and delineate how the new insights could be reconciled with feature-based approaches. In conclusion, complementing feature-based studies with studies targeting computational principles promises a comprehensive and mechanistic understanding of why certain visual stimuli are perceived as beautiful, and others are not.

articles_hidden.title: Testing the psychometric properties of depression and social-emotional functioning measures with autistic adolescents and their parents
articles_hidden.authors: My H Vu; Elika Parab; Vana Matevosian; Pia Hernandez; Jessica Schwartzman
articles_hidden.abstract: Autistic youth are a prevalent population in the U.S. facing greater risks for depression and adverse mental health outcomes than the general population of youth. The psychometric properties of most measures remain untested with autistic youth even though autism is characterized by significant heterogeneity including unique cognitive, affective, behavioral and sensory needs. The present study tested the internal consistency, confirmatory factor analysis, convergent and discriminant validity, and cross-informant agreement between 101 autistic adolescents (14-17 years old) and their parents for several depression and social-emotional functioning measures (e.g., social motivation, anhedonia/apathy). Most measures showed acceptable-to-good internal consistency across informants, while confirmatory factor analyses yielded mixed evidence of structural validity. Convergent validity was moderate and adolescent and parent reports agreed poorly to moderately, which emphasizes the value of collecting both perspectives. Findings inform clinical practice by supporting the continued use of several measures in autistic adolescents, while suggesting caution in interpreting others.

articles_hidden.title: Team Science: An Examination of Factors Associated with Citation Metrics
articles_hidden.authors: Kelly Cuccolo; Jordan Rose Wagge; John Edlund; Erin Michelle Buchanan
articles_hidden.abstract: Scientific collaboration, often measured through co-authorship, has grown in many disciplines and is frequently linked to increased citation rates. However, it remains unclear which disciplines have seen the greatest growth in collaboration and how this growth relates to article-level metrics. Moreover, little is known about how team demographics (e.g., h-index, gender, number of institutions) and team size interact with regard to research impact. Understanding these dynamics is essential given their influence on hiring, tenure, and the broader scientific ecosystem. Using metadata from Elsevier’s International Center for the Study of Research (ICSR) Lab, we examined collaboration trends across disciplines and their associations with citation outcomes. Team size increased over time, with variation by discipline, and was positively associated with citation counts. Gender relationships with citation rates varied by authorship order and discipline, indicating a complex relationship between gender and impact. Greater institutional and geographic diversity were linked to higher citation counts. Last authors’ h-indices were especially strongly associated with impact, particularly when self-citations were excluded. Effect sizes were small, and the observational design precludes causal conclusions. These findings describe how evolving patterns of collaboration are related to research visibility and underscore the importance of considering team composition, cautiously, in evaluations of scientific output.

articles_hidden.title: Rest-Activity Rhythms, Social Interaction, and Depressive Symptoms in Older Adults: A Longitudinal Within- and Between-Person Analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Kyungmi Lee; Jennifer B. Levin
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objectives: Rest-activity rhythm organization and social interaction have each been linked to late-life depression, yet their independent longitudinal contributions have rarely been examined within a framework separating between-person differences from within-person fluctuations. This study examined their independent associations with depressive symptoms in community-dwelling older adults.
Method: Data from Rounds 12–14 (2022–2024) of the National Health and Aging Trends Study (NHATS) included 1,532 person-wave observations from 606 participants. A Behavioral Rhythm Index (BRI) combined mean activity, relative amplitude, and reversed day-to-day variability. Person-mean-centered random-intercept linear mixed models separated within- from between-person associations, adjusting for wave, age, sex, and education.
Results: Higher BRI was associated with fewer depressive symptoms between persons (B = −0.238, p < .001) and within persons (B = −0.139, p = .013), although the within-person association was not robust across sensitivity analyses. Greater social interaction was associated with fewer depressive symptoms between persons (B = −0.714, p < .001) but not within persons. BRI and social interaction did not significantly interact (χ²(2) = 2.05, p = .359).
Conclusion: Higher BRI and greater habitual social engagement were each independently associated with fewer depressive symptoms between individuals, warranting further investigation as potentially modifiable behavioral factors in late-life depression.

articles_hidden.title: I Remember That Question: Using Eye Tracking to See How Prequestions Shape Reading
articles_hidden.authors: Jason Geller
articles_hidden.abstract:
Answering questions before learning (prequestions) improves memory for the information they
address, but how it does so is unclear. A common proposal is that prequestions direct attention to
that information. We tested this account by recording eye movements while participants read a
text about polio and tuberculosis after answering prequestions about one topic or none, so that
every target sentence was read both with and without prequestions. Prequestions improved
memory only for the prequestioned information, and eye movements showed the same
specificity. Ex-Gaussian models, which separate typical reading time from occasional unusually
long readings, showed that prequestions did not change typical reading of the answer sentences.
Instead, these sentences received more unusually long readings, were looked back to more often,
and were re-read for longer; other sentences were unaffected. Prequestions thus guide attention
selectively rather than heightening it, consistent with additional processing when readers
recognize an answer.

articles_hidden.title: Barriers to professional mental health help-seeking and considerations for school-based interventions among Secondary School adolescents: an exploratory qualitative study
articles_hidden.authors: Christianah Dada
articles_hidden.abstract:
ABSTRACT
Professional mental health service use remains low among adolescents, and school-based interventions are frequently designed without consulting the young people and clinicians they are intended to serve. This exploratory qualitative study investigated the specific barriers to professional mental health help-seeking among Nigerian adolescents to inform the development of a culturally relevant school-based intervention. Following the ethical principles of the Belmont Report, a focus group discussion was conducted with ten secondary school students (aged 13–16), alongside individual in-depth interviews with two students and key informant interviews with two practicing clinical psychologists in Ibadan, Nigeria. Audio-recorded transcripts were verified and examined utilizing thematic analysis. Eight core categories emerged from the data, highlighting a limited formal understanding of mental health among youth and a prominent gap between baseline knowledge and help-seeking behaviors. While distress including depression, anxiety, addiction, and trauma was widely recognized through behavioral or academic declines, pervasive stigma and the fear of diagnostic labeling acted as dominant barriers to care, with nine out of ten adolescents refusing professional care pathways. Friends served as primary confidants, while parental spiritual beliefs heavily gatekept formal psychological interventions. Social media heavily informed adolescent self-image but introduced acute body-image concerns. Notably, one student preferred using an artificial intelligence chatbot over human contact to ensure absolute confidentiality. Participants requested foundational mental health literacy and coping skills delivered via brief, visual, interactive sessions, while clinicians anticipated systemic institutional implementation challenges regarding school leadership, funding deficits, and staffing constraints. Interventions must target social stigma and privacy constraints directly alongside conceptual awareness.

articles_hidden.title: The Culture of Dissemblance Among Black American Women: A Mixed Methods Assessment
articles_hidden.authors: Linzie Taylor; Natalie Merril; Trinidi Prochaska; Amanda R. Arnold; Amy R Murphy; Megan E. Huibregtse; Angela Li; Abigail Powers; Vasiliki Michopoulos; Jennifer Stevens
articles_hidden.abstract: Disparities in the treatment of mood and stress disorders like posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) may partially reflect a limited culturally informed understanding of emotional processing. The culture of dissemblance (COD) describes how American Black women learned to mask their emotional expression as a protective mechanism within a society that places them at greater risk of psychosocial stressors while invalidating their emotional experience. This mixed methods study examined COD among forty-nine Black women (ages 40–55), who completed a semi-structured interview assessing emotional engagement alongside self-report measures of emotion regulation, trauma exposure, PTSD symptoms, racial discrimination, and Black identity. Thematic analysis indicated that participants experienced negative judgments of their emotional expression and learned to monitor emotional responses for self-protection. 83.7% of women reported less emotional expression in public with 40.8% of women identified the workplace as the primary site for emotional masking. Interview-based COD endorsement associated with belief in negative public perception of Black people but not with the other variables of interests. Treatment approaches should center Black women's cultural knowledge to address mental health disparities.

articles_hidden.title: Does autonomy enhance satisfaction, adherence and clinical outcomes? A Randomized Controlled Trial of a digital mental health intervention for college students
articles_hidden.authors: Sevin Ozmen; Leonore de Wit; Arpana Amarnath; Annemieke van Straten; Sascha Y Struijs
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: College students face high rates of mental health problems including depression and stress. Digital interventions offer accessible support, but adherence remains challenging. Autonomy may enhance motivation, yet its role in student-focused digital interventions is not explored yet in a randomized controlled trial. 
Objective: This study examines whether enhancing autonomy in a guided digital CBT-based mental health intervention for college students (LifeHack) improves satisfaction, adherence, and mental health outcomes.
Methods: In a two-armed randomized trial, 575 students were assigned to either a structured intervention or an autonomy-enhanced version in which participants could select topics of interest.
